articles.title: Brazil’s Far-Right Trajectory Is a Warning for Us All
articles.author: Rodrigo Nunes
articles.content: Attempts to make generalizations from what happens in the United States and Europe to the rest of the planet do not, as a rule, meet with much surprise; these are, after all, generally assumed to be the most advanced edges of world history, where processes that will eventually spread to other regions first take hold. Most of the literature on the lethal danger surrounding democracies that has flourished in the last decade implicitly assumes these central countries as the normative standard from which others — and increasingly themselves — can be measured as deviations. Starting from a place like Brazil, on the other hand, does not enjoy the same air of self-evidence and seems to require some explaining. Countries on the periphery are supposed to be somehow quirky and unique, partaking in what is universal only through the ways in which they have caught up with their developed counterparts, and otherwise assumed to be locked in a particularity that prevents them from offering anything generalizable. The irony, in this case, is that a tradition within Brazilian social thought has for some time elaborated an argument not only as to why that is not true but that those may, in fact, be precisely the places from where to start. After the defeat of historical fascism in World War II, the division of the world into two competing geopolitical blocs pushed both sides to work on their sales pitch to those countries that had hitherto lain in the margins of the global market. Whereas the Soviet bloc offered the international comradeship of the exploited and the imminence of world revolution, its capitalist rivals held up the promise that, if they stayed the free-market course, all nations could one day attain the same level of material well-being that the richest countries enjoyed. This prospect was at the center of the different approaches that became collectively known from the 1950s onward as “modernization theory.” Almost immediately, a loose group of thinkers from Latin America and Africa began to build a critique of it. Development was not a race, they argued, in which each country had their own lane to run down and could reach the finishing line regardless of when they began, but rather more like chess, the position of each piece conditioning the moves available to all others. This gave the first countries to set out on the capitalist road a first-mover advantage: While their own early takeoff had been made possible by colonialism and slavery (and the access to cheap labor and nature that these afforded), the integration of former colonies into the global market had been based on unequal exchange from the start, subordinating whatever development they could have to the needs and interests of development taking place elsewhere. The fact that one could speak of a center and a periphery within capitalism was, therefore, no mere factual, transient contingency. Not only had the constitution of the subordinate pole been the exact same process through which the dominant one established itself, but the fact that the former could only grow within terms dictated by the growth of the latter meant that, even as the periphery progressed, the very relation of dependency reproduced itself. This entailed that the development of the periphery could only ever be “dependent,” “limited,” or “underdeveloped.” That was not all. The assumption that modernization in all spheres of life — political institutions, labor relations, culture — would follow naturally from economic progress was simply not true. As Francisco de Oliveira’s classic text from the early 1970s put it, in a place like Brazil, “capitalist expansion takes place . . . through the introduction of new relations in the archaic and the reproduction of the archaic in the new”: “a symbiosis and organicity, a unity of contraries, in which the ‘modern’ thrives and feeds off the ‘backward,’ if we still wish to retain those terms.” Thus, for example, in the country’s mushrooming urban centers, it was the spread of self-built informal settlements (“ favelization ”) and the offer of cheap services like domestic work (itself a legacy of slavery) that, compensating for insufficient accumulation and infrastructure, enabled the high pace of industrialization observed from the 1930s to the 1960s. But this dialectical twist on the dialectics of the modern and the archaic had a further twist in store. By the late 1980s, it was modernization tout court, not only in the postcolonial world, that was coming to seem a mirage. In capitalism’s very core, rights and institutions that had been thought to be everlasting achievements were being rolled back; from that point on, it would be ever clearer that astonishing material advancement could exist side by side with levels of exploitation and inequality until recently deemed to be part of the past. Economic growth was no longer a guarantee of any of the things that were supposed to come with it — including, increasingly, democracy. What if what had been mistaken as the inevitable march of progress, the direction toward which the arc of history bent, had in fact only been a blip produced by three decades of uninterrupted expansion after the war — and what the future had in store was, in fact, as some had begun to predict, a progressive “ Brazilianization ” of the world? If that were so, a group of Brazilian thinkers concluded, it was no longer just the case that the periphery was a space forever destined to be stuck between the future and the past. In its permanent, uneasy but organic, functionally dysfunctional amalgamation of the modern and the archaic, the developed and the under- or de-developed, it was, and had indeed always been, the future. “At the historical hour when the country of the future [Brazil] seems to no longer have any future,” Paulo Arantes wrote , “we are singled out, for better or worse, as the future of the world.” Not, and this was crucial, in the simple sense that the once modern core was backsliding, but rather in that, having been a society overpoweringly determined from the outset by the dictates of economic reason (its constitution as a locus of production for the nascent world system), Brazil foreshadowed a world in which brute exploitation became the ever more dominant social logic. “We are once again in the vanguard, except now of disintegration.” This “Brazilianization” (or, in more general terms, peripheralization) thesis states , in a nutshell, that “ the world’s horizon of expectation is no longer informed by the center, but by the peripheries.” That is, both by the peripherical areas that proliferate in the metropolises of a “ planet of slums ” and by the former colonies that have from birth been “perfect laboratories for new forms of capitalist exploitation integrating authoritarian control of surplus populations, the management of unresolvable social conflicts and a new police state compatible with parliamentary democracy.” (Gaza being, of course, the most extreme form yet experienced of such laboratories.) What this suggests is that the likes of Brazil, Argentina, El Salvador, and so on may actually help us see more clearly the direction in which the contemporary far right points than can places like the United States and Western Europe, whose still relatively dominant position in the international division of labor allows for promises of national redemption that dull and disguise the features of what is likely to come: the privately managed breakdown of a world beset by climate collapse, the rampant growth of inequality and superfluous populations, and the proliferation of protected enclaves, sacrificial zones, and areas of contested sovereignty at both the supra- and the infranational levels. articles.title: Hyman Minsky Was a Powerful Critic of Capitalism
articles.author: Riccardo Bellofiore
articles.content: Thirty years after Hyman Minsky’s death, his name is more familiar than his political economy. Whenever asset prices collapse, leverage suddenly matters, or a financial boom turns into panic, someone announces a new “Minsky moment.” The phrase has become shorthand for the point at which a speculative expansion can no longer sustain itself. Hedge finance turns into speculative finance, speculative finance into Ponzi finance, and a structure that appeared stable suddenly discovers that everybody cannot become liquid at the same time. This posthumous fame has narrowed our understanding of Minsky’s legacy . He was not primarily a prophet of crashes. Rather, he was a theorist of a capitalism that changes its institutional form, and of the ways financial instability itself helps produce those changes. He was also a severe critic of Keynesianism. That is the Minsky worth remembering today. Marx, Schumpeter, Keynes, and Minsky Minsky studied with Joseph Schumpeter at Harvard. He read the work of John Maynard Keynes as a theorist of a monetary production economy and was indirectly influenced by Karl Marx. Minsky characterized Schumpeter and Keynes as Marxist economists who were conservative and pro-capitalist. They were the “great dissenters”: economists who understood that capitalism cannot first be analyzed in “real” terms and only afterward supplied with money. Money is there from the beginning. More than that: money is not merely the most important thing; it is the only thing. Marx’s circuit of capital starts with money advanced as finance to production in order to buy labor power and means of production. Schumpeter made the monetary point even sharper: bank credit creates purchasing power ex nihilo and gives entrepreneurs command over resources before the results of their decisions are known. Keynes showed how investment depends on expectations concerning an unknowable future. Minsky brought these insights together by focusing on the interlocking balance sheets that connect money today to uncertain money tomorrow. Marx helps identify something Minsky leaves relatively underdeveloped. Finance for production gives firms command not simply over “resources” but over living labor power, i.e., human beings just regarded by capital as bearers of the capacity to work. The valorization process is a monetary process, a process of money bearing more money as abstract wealth. Monetary theory is not a theory of a separate financial sphere: it is a theory of capitalist production as a whole. Finance does not become important only after value has been produced. It helps determine in advance who gets to organize production, which technologies are adopted, how labor is organized, and which futures become economically possible. Stability Is Destabilizing Capitalism is a monetary economy built on promises about an uncertain future. Firms invest today because they expect future cash flows. To do so, they incur debts carrying contractual payments, whether or not those expectations are realized. The same logic applies, in different forms, to households and financial institutions. A financially robust unit can meet interest and principal out of its expected cash receipts. Minsky called this hedge finance. A speculative unit can pay interest but must refinance to cover the principal. A Ponzi unit cannot even meet current financial charges without further borrowing, capital gains, or refinancing. The crucial point is that fragility is produced inside the expansion itself. After a crisis, lenders and borrowers are cautious. As prosperity continues, yesterday’s risks are validated. Practices once regarded as dangerous appear safe, and financial institutions compete by inventing ways around existing constraints. Prolonged tranquility, or a technological wave generating exceptional expected returns, endogenously reduces the margins of safety previously regarded as prudent. This is what Minsky meant when he remarked that stability is destabilizing. His theory is not simply one of irrational exuberance. Successful financial practices change the institutions and conventions through which finance operates. The canonical version of the argument has a problem. Minsky often described the boom as one in which nonfinancial firms progressively increase their leverage to finance investment. That makes sense for an individual firm. But it cannot simply be generalized to firms as a whole. Here Minsky’s own debt to Michał Kalecki becomes important. Investment expenditure generates profits. When one firm borrows and spends, another firm receives revenue. The attempt by individual firms to increase debt does not therefore imply that the corporate sector as a whole must become increasingly indebted. This is not a reason to discard Minsky. It is a reason to read his Financial Instability Hypothesis as a tendency, one which is quite often overcome by countertendencies (as in the case of Marx’s law of the falling rate of profit). The pressure toward fragility can be displaced. That is exactly what happened in the decades before 2007. Nonfinancial corporations were not always the most fragile part of the system. Leverage migrated toward financial intermediaries and households. Household debt, especially mortgage debt, became central to the expansion. The subprime mortgage market was almost a textbook Ponzi position: its viability depended on continuously rising house prices and the ability to refinance. The “Minsky moment” of 2007 was therefore not simply the end of a speculative episode. It was the breakdown of a stage of capitalism. There is another side of Kalecki that matters. His 1943 argument on the political barriers to full employment can be read as a labor theory of value in disguise. Permanent full employment changes the balance of power inside production: workers become less afraid of dismissal, workplace discipline weakens, wage claims strengthen, and capital begins to resist policies that may remain perfectly compatible with aggregate profitability. Kalecki thus brings the conflict over the extraction and distribution of surplus value back inside the macroeconomic theory of effective demand. In doing so, he anticipates what happened at the end of the 1960s and the beginning of the 1970s: a crisis of the capital-labor relation. From One Capitalism to Another Minsky developed a theory of capitalism unfolding in stages that distinguished between commercial, industrial, financial, managerial, and finally money manager capitalism. Each form of capitalism develops its own financial institutions, relations of power, and characteristic sources of instability. As in Marx and Schumpeter, the destabilization of one stage gives rise to the next. Capitalism is an evolutionary system that continually transforms the institutional conditions of its own reproduction. In commercial capitalism, finance was connected with trade and working capital. Industrial capitalism greatly expanded the need to finance long-lived fixed investment and, with it, the importance of investment banks and securities markets. Financial capitalism concentrated power in financiers, large shareholders, and increasingly large corporations. In 1929, the Great Crash set off a collapse of capitalism that was not overcome until World War II. Afterward, in the stage of managerial capitalism, private balance sheets were relatively strong. Big government deficits supported aggregate profits and employment. Large corporations could rely heavily on internal finance, and managers acquired considerable autonomy from shareholders and bankers. The institutions that at first stabilized managerial capitalism ultimately transformed but also destabilized it. Professional money managers at pension funds, mutual funds, and other institutional investors came to control corporate securities. The criterion of success was the appreciation of the managed assets. The result was money manager capitalism. This was not merely a question of finance having a bigger role in the economy. Finance changed production itself. Corporate management became increasingly sensitive to stock-market valuation, and leveraged buyouts, mergers, outsourcing, downsizing, and cost compression reorganized firms. Vertically integrated corporations gave way to networks and supply chains, while employment became less secure and more precarious. I have dubbed this phase the “real subsumption of labor to finance”: any resemblance to Marxian terminology is not purely coincidental. So-called financialization should not be imagined as a parasitic sphere sitting above a separate “real economy.” Financial criteria enter production, as required returns are transmitted into the labor process through processes of restructuring, outsourcing, work intensification, and employment insecurity. The process may also be a push to accelerate innovation and raise the productive power of labor. This regime simultaneously produces traumatized workers, manic-depressive savers embedded in financial markets through pensions and property, and indebted consumers. The connection between the latter two runs through a loop linking monetary policy to capital-asset inflation. The rising apparent value of past savings favors a decline in saving out of current income, which may become negative. Rising asset prices could partially compensate, for a while, for weak wage growth, because households borrowed against housing and financial wealth. This configuration amounted to a form of privatized Keynesianism. Instead of the state directly sustaining demand through public expenditure, private debt and asset inflation did much of the work. Central banks supported the mechanism by repeatedly providing liquidity and protecting financial markets from collapse, increasingly acting as lenders of first resort. The result could be dynamic for a time. Finance itself became a countertendency to stagnation. This was neither a stagnationist nor a laissez-faire form of capitalism: it was a very politically driven capitalism. But it generated dynamism by once again creating the conditions for a larger transformation and crisis. The apparent stability of the Great Moderation allowed leverage to rise elsewhere in the system. Cushions of safety appeared to improve because collateral values kept rising. When house prices stopped rising, the entire structure reversed. That is why calling 2007 a “Minsky moment” misses the point. It was the culmination of what L. Randall Wray and Eric Tymoigne have called a Minsky half-century. What Comes After? What is generally referred to as the “2008 crisis,” associated with Lehman Brothers, actually began the previous year with the subprime crash. It had been anticipated by the dot-com collapse at the beginning of the decade. For a few months, “neoliberalism” appeared to be dead: and it was, in that form. Banks were rescued, deficits exploded, and central banks abandoned any pretense that financial markets could be left to themselves. But what followed was not a new progressive settlement. It was a zombie interlude: the private financial structure was rescued while austerity was imposed on much of the population. Meanwhile the ecological crisis increasingly clouded the horizon. The pandemic and the health crisis finally broke the political-economic pattern inherited from the post-2007 interregnum. After 2020, active fiscal policy returned on a scale that had been ruled out for decades. Governments ran enormous deficits, and states provided guarantees, subsidies, industrial policy, infrastructure spending, and support for green and digital investment. Calling this the “return of the state” is, however, misleading, since the state never left. What changed was the form of intervention. I would describe the regime that actually materialized as a second generation of privatized Keynesianism. The first generation, between roughly 1987 and 2007, supported demand through private debt, asset inflation, and central bank guarantees. The second supports demand much more directly through public deficits and the state balance sheet. However, the crucial asymmetry remains: demand is publicly supported, while the criteria governing allocation, production, and the labor market remain private and oriented toward hit-and-run profitability. Risk is socialized while returns remain private. Industrial policy subsidizes strategic corporations, digital platforms, military-industrial complexes, and reorganized supply chains without any true public and democratic control. Employment can rise without undoing fragmented and precarious labor relations. Public money increasingly guarantees the future profitability of private investment. A Critic of Keynesianism The most surprising Minsky is, however, the political Minsky. He was a Keynesian, but he did not believe postwar Keynesianism had fulfilled Keynes’s radical potential. His starting point was Keynes’s famous call for a “somewhat comprehensive socialisation of investment.” Keynes concluded that monetary policy alone could not guarantee enough private investment to secure full employment. But he immediately limited the argument. The fundamental defect of capitalism, he maintained, concerned the volume rather than the direction of employment. Once resources were fully employed, even the Keynes who supported the socialization of investment wrote that the market allocated them reasonably well and that neoclassical theory retained a local validity. Minsky, like Joan Robinson before him, asked a much sharper question: Full employment for what? Once Keynesian policy had shown that full employment was politically possible, the composition of employment and production could no longer be treated as a secondary issue. The question was not merely whether everybody could be put to work, but what they would be producing, under what conditions, and for whom. The same problem runs through the later critique of military Keynesianism, organized waste, and induced private consumption (here Minsky is on the same page as Paul Baran and Paul Sweezy). Big Government and Big Finance could prevent another great collapse. But they could do so while stabilizing a conservative form of capitalism based on high profits, large corporations, military expenditure, induced private investment, and ever-expanding private consumption. Minsky’s answer was not simply “more Keynes.” He returned instead to Franklin Delano Roosevelt and the New Deal, in a kind of left idealization of it. While the New Deal might have lacked Keynes’s theory of effective demand, it had something postwar Keynesianism had lost, structural reform — a banner that is suicidal to leave to the Right. It reformed finance, created institutions against debt deflation, and provided direct employment to fulfill social needs. Minsky wanted to combine Keynesian effective demand with New Deal structural reform. That is why his employer-of-last-resort proposal should not be reduced to a technical job guarantee mechanism. He wanted full employment, but he also wanted public employment to produce goods and services outside the immediate criterion of private profitability. He wanted expenditure to be targeted. The point is that the composition of output itself must become a political question. At points, Minsky went very far. He argued that control over the finance committees of large corporations could open a route toward decentralized socialism, or toward guided interventionist capitalism. Beyond Stabilizing an Unstable Economy This is where Minsky’s work remains unfinished. If finance determines which firms obtain purchasing power before production begins, finance already exercises a kind of private social planning (Schumpeter’s point). It gives some actors the possibility of hiring labor power, mobilizing productive resources, introducing technologies, and determining the material shape of a future that has not yet arrived. Wealth, in capitalism, is not merely the possibility of consuming more. It is power over the direction of the future (Keynes’s point). That is why the socialization of investment eventually raises a larger question: the socialization of the use of productive capacity. If you wish, there is a hint directing us toward an economy of social production. This does not mean a bureaucratic command economy. It means refusing to treat private profitability as the only mechanism that can decide what is produced, how it is produced, and for whom. And it means taking the organization of labor seriously. A democratic decision over what to produce is incomplete if workers remain subordinated inside production itself. The ecological crisis drives home the same point still more sharply. Financial claims can be refinanced, and balance sheets can be restructured, but a destroyed ecosystem cannot be rolled over. Nor can we restore living labor power that has already been consumed and damaged. The material irreversibility of the use of workers and nature cannot be abolished by rearranging monetary claims. The Minsky recurrently made fashionable at each new crisis gave his name to a financial panic. The more radical Minsky understood that financial instability — and the unsustainability of capitalist processes more broadly, even when they are temporarily stable — is generated by capitalism’s always changing forms. Stabilizing capitalism without changing its structure may simply pave the way for the next crisis. articles.title: Israel’s Rogue State Behavior Is Somehow Only Worsening
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: I t is not a novel point that Israel acts like a rogue state , or that its behavior toward the United States often more closely resembles the behavior of an adversary than that of an ally. But it’s still worth periodically noting just how extreme its misbehavior on the world stage is, given that it is underwritten by the US taxpayers, even as majorities of Americans don’t want it to be. Let’s just keep it to things that have happened roughly this past week; otherwise this piece could end up being the length of a medium-sized book. There was the incident where illegal Israeli settlers in the West Bank — who are financed , armed , enabled , and otherwise supported in every possible way by the Israeli government — viciously attacked a Washington Post photojournalist, breaking her ribs and fracturing her vertebrae, and a day later attacked a group of European diplomats from Belgium, France, and Poland (countries that, unlike Israel, actually are US treaty allies). The reaction was, well, muted. The Israeli government at first tried to cast doubt on the reports, accuse Palestinians of being the culprits, and even blame the diplomats. The US secretary of state said it was “not a good look.” The German government called it “troubling” and said it should “be criticized,” while the European Union called vaguely for “full accountability.” The Israeli government did arrest ten suspects and has now released nine of them from custody and into house arrest. Given that merely bringing charges against a group of Israeli soldiers who gang-raped a Palestinian prisoner led to Israeli rioting , which then led to those charges being dropped and one of the rapists becoming a quasi-celebrity in the country, don’t hold your breath waiting for this accountability. At the same time, Israel continues to violate ceasefire agreements at will in the multiple wars in neighboring countries it’s fighting, routinely killing innocent civilians. In Gaza, it has in recent days killed a ten-year-old boy, a young girl , a seventeen-year-old , and a married couple, among others. These are just a small fraction of the more than 1,500 Palestinians it has killed in the territory since it signed a ceasefire last year — a death toll that alone is higher than the number of Israelis killed, both civilian and military, on October 7, 2023. Israel is also still bombing Lebanon, another place where it signed a ceasefire months ago yet continues to attack anyway, and where its soldiers are still demolishing entire villages and posting videos cheerfully mocking their victims. This behavior isn’t limited to low-level grunts. The Israeli defense minister has launched a flurry of threats against Lebanon, including to carry out more bombings on its capital, to illegally seize more of its land, and to displace a million people. Lebanon is only one of Israel’s neighbors whose territory it is illegally occupying, where it has imposed restrictions on the behavior of the local population. Another is Syria, where it launched a series of ground raids and set a curfew and other restrictions on a set of villages this week. This is not counting Palestinian territories, where Israeli officials are flagrantly defying international law and world opinion by occupying and calling for the annexation of Gaza and by gradually annexing the West Bank through the very violent settlers responsible for those shocking attacks last week. Eight of nine Israeli political parties earlier this month rejected the idea of an independent Palestinian state, going against what has been the overwhelming global consensus for decades and effectively committing to a one-state solution of explicit apartheid, with Israel controlling territory holding five million Palestinians without granting them basic rights like voting. (The one party that didn’t reject it was cut off by a bad connection.) Oh, and the Israeli prime minister is vowing to carry out regime change in an entirely different country, Iran, which he is reportedly actively making plans to attack next month after the US elections. Less than two weeks ago, a former Israeli military intelligence chief laid out for a prominent Israeli think tank the country’s new security doctrine — not what he thought it should be, or what some officials are working to make it, but what it already is based on the country’s actions the past few years. The core planks: the subordination of democracy to ethnonationalism, a state of permanent war with the entire Arab world, pursuit of preemptive sneak attacks as a matter of policy, and a rejection of Arab neighbors’ sovereignty coupled with the need to destabilize them. So, in summary, the Israeli government is: complicit in violent attacks on Western countries’ citizens and government officials; routinely and flagrantly violating ceasefire agreements and international law; having its officials make wild, explicit threats of bombing and ethnic cleansing; waging or plotting war on at least three of its neighbors (four counting Palestine); and illegally occupying or planning to seize their land — all as it plans a future as an undemocratic ethnostate launching never-ending preemptive wars on the entire Arab world. And this is just covering the past week or so. We can add all this to the numerous other violations Israel has racked up the past few years: its literal war on the United Nations, attacks on diplomatic facilities, assassination of foreign officials and negotiators, or, of course, the widely recognized genocide it’s carried out, to name a few. And now, it’s set to get much worse, as the Israeli government yesterday jumped on the shooting of two soldiers in the West Bank — a shooting that follows years of intensifying Israeli military and settler violence and destruction aimed at Palestinians there — to launch what it calls a Gaza-like war on the West Bank and quite possibly kill the two-state solution for good. There are plenty of countries doing terrible things in the world — just look at Russia’s pitiless bombardment of Ukraine or Saudi Arabia’s renewed destruction of Yemen. But there is no other country that you can say all of the above about, whose rap sheet even comes close to the length and breadth of Israel’s recent violations. If Israel were an official US adversary, it would have been hit with an ever-growing pile of sanctions long ago, and we would be hearing constant demands for war against it — which, to be clear, would be a disastrous course of action here, but one that the United States and Europe have taken for much less than what Israel is currently doing. Instead, the Israeli state does not even receive a slap on the wrist. Worse, actually, as Washington and most of Europe’s capitals continue to stubbornly arm or provide diplomatic and economic support to Israel as it does all this, effectively supporting the very behavior they would never accept from any other country, and a policy most of their own citizens disagree with. And so it goes on, with no end in sight. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Pressure Campaigns
articles.author: Guest Author
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. What happens when activists stop asking corporations to do the right thing and start making it expensive for them to do the wrong thing? That question was at the heart of “Pressure Campaigns: The Power of Boycotts and Direct Action,” a panel at the fourth annual Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4, 2026, at Cal State Los Angeles. Moderated by MaryLinda Moss , artist, activist, and founding member of NELA Alliance for Democracy, the discussion brought together Miriam Arghandiwal , an organizer with the Boycott Home Depot Coalition and Entertainment Labor for Palestine; Chris Abrahamsen , co-founder of Grassroots Activist International Association and regional director of ICEBreakers; and Robby Kumar , a former investment banker and congressional staffer working with De-ICE Citizens Bank and No Camps California. Their campaigns target different industries, but share a central premise: Corporations respond to financial incentives, public scrutiny, and the possibility of losing customers, investors, and business relationships. The panelists described how ordinary people can use those vulnerabilities to challenge institutions with vastly greater financial and political resources. Boycotts and Pressure Campaigns (1:21:03) Home Depot: When the Workplace Becomes an ICE Target Arghandiwal described the Boycott Home Depot Coalition's campaign against the retailer over immigration enforcement raids targeting day laborers in its parking lots. The boycott, initiated by Unión del Barrio, calls on Home Depot to publicly condemn ICE operations, prevent immigration enforcement activities on its properties where legally possible, provide safe hiring areas for day laborers, compensate affected families, and remove surveillance equipment and devices intended to discourage people from gathering. Arghandiwal said organizers have documented more than 700 people taken into custody in connection with Home Depot locations across Southern California. But she emphasized that pressure campaigns must protect the very people they are intended to support. Demonstrations at stores where day laborers gather can inadvertently attract additional law enforcement, putting vulnerable workers at greater risk. The coalition therefore developed guidelines requiring organizers to consult day laborers before staging protests and, when appropriate, conduct demonstrations at locations or times that minimize those risks. The campaign has also pursued divestment. Arghandiwal reported that organizers helped secure the withdrawal of $20 million in Illinois investment funds from Home Depot and a smaller divestment commitment in West Hollywood. These actions illustrate how consumer boycotts can extend into public investment decisions, increasing pressure beyond individual purchasing choices. Hollywood: Boycotts as Cultural Resistance Arghandiwal also discussed Entertainment Labor for Palestine, which organizes in support of the Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement. Unlike conventional consumer campaigns, Hollywood pressure campaigns often focus on cultural influence, public reputation, and accountability within the entertainment industry. Organizers have demonstrated at the Academy Awards, protested film premieres, and challenged entertainment companies over their treatment of artists who publicly support Palestinian rights. Arghandiwal cited protests surrounding Scream 7 , following the firing of actress Melissa Barrera over social media statements concerning Gaza. She described efforts to sustain public attention throughout the film's promotional campaign, including demonstrations at its premiere. Entertainment Labor for Palestine also participated in protests surrounding Disney productions, including Captain America: Brave New World and Snow White . For Arghandiwal, success is not measured exclusively in immediate box-office losses. Changing what studios, executives, and performers consider reputationally acceptable can influence future decisions even when the financial consequences are difficult to calculate. Her broader argument was that sustained publ Spotify: Eleven Weeks of Pressure Chris Abrahamsen offered one of the panel's clearest examples of a campaign with a specific corporate demand and a reported measurable outcome. When Spotify began running ICE recruitment advertisements, organizers quickly mobilized demonstrations demanding that the streaming platform stop carrying them. Abrahamsen described a campaign involving weekly protests outside Spotify offices, extensive outreach to musicians, and highly visible demonstrations using washable simulated blood to symbolize the suffering organizers associated with immigration enforcement. The coalition also encouraged consumers to switch to competing streaming services. An important part of the strategy involved what Abrahamsen called tertiary targets : influential people or organizations capable of pressuring the corporation even when its executives refused to engage directly. In Spotify's case, those targets included musicians whose participation was essential to the platform's business. After approximately 11 weeks, Spotify stopped running the advertisements. Abrahamsen attributed the outcome to sustained organizing, although he acknowledged that Spotify did not publicly credit the protests for its decision. He estimated that the advertising contract was worth approximately $78,000, compared with roughly $2,000 in campaign materials. For the organizers, the episode d Hilton: Making Corporate Contracts Costly Following the Spotify campaign, Abrahamsen's organizing network turned its attention to Hilton hotels over accommodations provided to immigration enforcement personnel. The campaign demands that Hilton refuse room bookings paid for with government purchasing cards associated with ICE or the Department of Homeland Security and disclose the financial extent of those arrangements. Organizers have staged repeated demonstrations at Hilton properties, including actions inside hotel lobbies. Unlike Spotify, where customers could easily switch streaming platforms, Hilton presents a more complicated target involving individual properties, hotel management, and government purchasing arrangements. Abrahamsen argued that demonstrations generate costs beyond the immediate disruption: additional security, staffing, management attention, and the potential loss of customers. He stressed the importance of choosing campaigns with achievable demands and maintaining pressure until those demands are addressed. The strategic calculation, as he described it, is whether organizers can make continued corporate participation in a disputed activity more expensive than withdrawing from it. Citizens Bank: Following the Institutional Money Robby Kumar brought a different perspective to the discussion. Drawing on his background in investment banking, he explained why targeting individual customers is only one way to pressure financial institutions. De-ICE Citizens Bank has challenged Citizens Bank over its financial relationships with private prison corporations GEO Group and CoreCivic. While activists initially concentrated on convincing individual customers to withdraw deposits and close accounts, Kumar encouraged a focus on municipal governments and other institutional banking customers. The potential financial impact was substantially greater. According to Kumar, Jersey City approved withdrawing approximately $265 million from Citizens Bank, while Montclair, New Jersey, moved to withdraw another $91 million. He also cautioned against prematurely declaring victory. When Citizens Bank announced that it would discontinue certain lending facilities involving the private prison companies, some organizers considered the campaign successful. Kumar disagreed with treating that announcement as a complete break. He argued that changes in the companies' financing needs, following federal purchases of detention facilities, complicated the significance of the bank's decision. Citizens Bank had not necessarily ended every financial relationship with the companies. His lesson was important: A campaign must define success precisely enough to distinguish a substantive corporate change from a public-relations announcement. Building Coalitions Without Endangering Communities Throughout the discussion, speakers returned to the importance of organizing across movements. The campaigns against immigration enforcement, corporate financing, and Israel's treatment of Palestinians frequently intersect through shared institutions, contractors, and financial relationships. But coalition building requires judgment. Arghandiwal emphasized that confrontational demonstrations may be inappropriate when they expose day laborers or undocumented communities to additional danger. Abrahamsen similarly explained that disruptive action groups sometimes need to operate separately from organizations providing direct services to vulnerable immigrants. Cooperation does not require identical tactics. Instead, effective coalitions can share research, coordinate messaging, identify financial pressure points, and support one another while respecting the different risks facing their members. Turning Outrage Into Organized Power The panel concluded with practical lessons about strategy. Successful pressure campaigns, the speakers suggested, begin by identifying who makes the decisions, what those decision-makers value, which relationships give others leverage over them, and what specific concessions would constitute a victory. They also require persistence, creativity, public visibility, and a willingness to adapt. The discussion demonstrated that economic resistance is not limited to refusing purchases. It can involve persuading municipalities to move millions in public deposits, pressuring artists to challenge streaming platforms, demanding accountability from entertainment companies, or organizing customers around corporate contracts. The larger lesson of the Left Coast Forum panel was that power does not reside exclusively in corporate boardrooms or government offices. Consumers, workers, artists, investors, and communities also exercise economic power. The challenge is to organize that power collectively, strategically, and long enough to make a difference.

articles.title: The Impact of ICE
articles.author: Guest Author
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A mother detained while seeking her green card. A woman arrested outside her home in pajamas and slippers. A transgender immigrant forced to choose between prolonged isolation and the threat of violence. A 60-year-old woman imprisoned for months after immigration agents allegedly mistook her for a 25-year-old. These were not hypothetical scenarios. They were among the experiences described by immigrant rights advocates at the fourth annual Left Coast Forum , held October 2–4, 2026, at California State University, Los Angeles. The panel, “The Impact of ICE: The Fight to Shut Down the Concentration Camps in California,” brought together organizers confronting the expansion of immigration detention, the growing influence of private prison corporations, and the erosion of constitutional protections. Facilitated by NO Concentration Camps CA and moderated by artist and activist MaryLinda Moss , the discussion featured Jeannie Parent , coordinator of Kern Welcoming and Extending Solidarity to Immigrants (KWESI); Bertie Hernandez , an undocumented transgender organizer working with the Dignity Not Detention Coalition; and Cal Soto , Workers’ Rights Director and Staff Attorney at the National Day Laborer Organizing Network (NDLON). Together, they described a system they believe is designed not simply to detain immigrants, but to extract profit from their incarceration while making resistance increasingly difficult. Families Torn Apart, Lives Put on Hold Jeannie Parent has been visiting people in immigration detention since 2015, when the Mesa Verde detention facility opened in Bakersfield. Through KWESI, volunteers visit incarcerated immigrants, provide money for food and telephone calls, and help arrange transportation, clothing, and shelter when people are released. Parent described a woman from Utah who was detained after stepping outside her home in pajamas and slippers. She had been caring for a daughter undergoing cancer treatment and a husband recovering from a kidney transplant. She spent eight months detained in California City. Another woman came from India on a student visa, earned a nursing degree, married, and had a baby. During an interview concerning her immigration status, she was separated from her husband, handcuffed, and detained for eight months. When released, she told Parent that she was grateful she had introduced her six-month-old baby to bottle-feeding before her arrest, allowing her family to care for the child. Parent rejected the government's portrayal of detained immigrants as the "worst of the worst." "These are nursing mothers, our neighbors, our friends," she told the audience. During the first seven months of 2026, Parent reported, KWESI provided $50 commissary deposits to approximately 700 people and helped more than 200 individuals through visits and other assistance. When Human Confinement Becomes a Business The panelists repeatedly returned to the financial incentives sustaining immigration detention. Companies such as GEO Group and CoreCivic operate detention facilities under government contracts, creating a system in which public money supports privately operated incarceration. According to the panelists, people held inside face inadequate food, expensive communications, restrictive visitation, and considerable obstacles to obtaining legal assistance. Parent described California City's detention facility, which she said held at least 2,200 people, as operating much like a maximum-security prison. The financial exploitation continues even after release. Soto described people leaving detention without telephones, transportation, or money, sometimes after spending months purchasing necessities from prison commissaries. The contradiction is especially troubling for advocates. They raise money to help people survive confinement, knowing some of those funds ultimately benefit the companies operating the facilities. The panelists argued that this arrangement creates a disturbing incentive: The longer people remain incarcerated, the more money detention operators may receive. A Transgender Organizer Confronts the System That Imprisoned Them For Bertie Hernandez, immigration detention is not an abstract political issue. Hernandez described spending approximately four months detained at Adelanto during Donald Trump's first administration. As a transgender person, Hernandez confronted an impossible choice: Accept isolation for approximately 23 hours each day or enter a detention population where their personal safety could be threatened. Hernandez chose the latter, explaining that prolonged isolation posed its own profound psychological dangers. That experience helped shape their commitment to organizing alongside detained transgender, queer, and gender-variant immigrants. Hernandez challenged the assumption that the system could be repaired simply through better management or improved detention conditions. From their feminist abolitionist perspective, the problem is structural. Racism, economic exploitation, gender-based violence, and incarceration reinforce one another. Rather than asking the public to recognize the humanity of immigrants, Hernandez turned the question around: Why must incarcerated people continually prove they deserve humane treatment? The moral responsibility, they suggested, rests with those willing to tolerate their mistreatment. Fighting ICE in Court—and Beyond Cal Soto described how NDLON, a national network of more than 70 day laborer worker centers, has expanded its work from fighting wage theft and workplace exploitation to challenging immigration raids and detention. Soto discussed litigation involving warrantless arrests and discriminatory immigration enforcement practices. In one case, a federal judge ordered the release of a 60-year-old woman who had been detained since April. According to Soto, government records indicated that agents were looking for someone approximately 25 years old. Soto also discussed litigation challenging immigration enforcement practices in Southern California, including raids targeting day laborers. The legal campaign incorporated more than 100 declarations from people describing their encounters with immigration agents. Importantly, Soto emphasized that the affected workers were participants in developing the litigation strategy, not merely witnesses called upon to support attorneys' arguments. Although courts have sometimes provided meaningful relief, Soto warned against depending on judges alone to protect vulnerable communities. Legal victories matter, but organized communities make those victories possible—and help turn individual cases into broader campaigns for justice. What Can One Person Do? Perhaps the most practical discussion came when an audience member asked how organizers should respond to people who feel overwhelmed, emotionally exhausted, or powerless. Parent suggested beginning with something as simple as writing a letter to a detained immigrant. For someone who has spent months without receiving a visitor, a letter can provide reassurance that the outside world has not forgotten them. Other opportunities include contributing commissary funds, providing transportation after release, creating artwork for demonstrations, contacting elected officials, or participating in organized protests. Hernandez emphasized that anger need not lead to helplessness. It can become a force for action and transformation. Soto offered another perspective: Effective movements require discipline and continuity, not simply moments of inspiration. He compared organizing to a musical composition containing notes too long for one singer to sustain. Another voice must enter as the first falls silent. The movement continues because people support one another. From Individual Resistance to Collective Power As the discussion concluded, Moss emphasized the importance of connecting organizations across California, building coalitions, and sustaining public pressure against detention facilities. The organizers made clear that the fight is not simply about improving conditions inside immigration detention centers. Their objective is to shut them down. But their work also poses a broader question: What does it say about a society when incarcerating people generates corporate profits while providing adequate food, housing, healthcare, and legal representation remains a struggle? The panel offered no easy solution to a system sustained by enormous political and economic power. Instead, it presented something more practical: a model of resistance built through collective action, mutual aid, legal challenges, public education, and solidarity with those most directly harmed. The session ended with a call-and-response that captured its central message: “What's stronger than a fascist?” “The power of the masses!”

articles.title: There’s No End in Sight to Yemen’s Destructive War
articles.author: Helen Lackner
articles.content: Yet again, the world is failing to give Yemen the attention it deserves. Well over a month into the renewal of the war between Ansar Allah, known as the Huthis, and the internationally recognized government (IRG), there have already been thousands of military and civilian casualties on both sides. Fierce fighting is going on in different parts of the country, and more than 250,000 people have been displaced, most of whom are moving from one active front line to areas that might be swept up in the conflict within hours. The humanitarian situation is disastrous, with famine threatening in some parts of the country. One of Yemen’s largest cities, Taiz, is under siege by the Huthis, with hardly any medical supplies, food, or water arriving for the population, now swollen by the 120,000 or so people displaced within the governorate. All of this deserves to be the focus of international concern. The return of full-scale fighting in Yemen was expected. Throughout the country, few favored continuation of the “no war, no peace” situation that had prevailed since the 2022 temporary truce. Despite this, the main events to have grabbed the headlines are the few Huthi drones and missiles that successfully attacked airports and some oil facilities in Riyadh and other locations in Saudi Arabia. Admittedly, these attacks have killed close to twenty people and wounded more than three hundred, and they are an important political development for the kingdom. They also demonstrate that the regional conflict has expanded way beyond both Gaza and Iran, thanks to Donald Trump’s recklessness in going to war in support of Benjamin Netanyahu’s projects. While there is a clear link between the Iran war and what is going on in Yemen and Saudi Arabia, the issues in the two centers of conflict are distinct, and each could exist without the other. But are lives lost in Riyadh worth more than those in Taiz or Sana’a? Back to War Since July 2026, the war in Yemen has resumed at a fiercer and more destructive tempo than its original outbreak in 2015. Fighting on the ground is costing hundreds of lives, mainly among the Huthi troops whose leaders are sending waves of young and inexperienced fighters, many of whom were forcibly recruited, to the front lines in pursuit of their offensive. Fighting continues in the northern areas of Marib and Sa’ada bordering Saudi Arabia. In early September, Ansar Allah took control of the southern part of the Yemeni coast, including both the Bab al-Mandab Strait and Mokha. It achieved this rapid victory thanks to three main factors: its own command efficiency, continued division and lack of coordination among its opponents, and the use of advanced technology, including artificial intelligence misinformation systems. The period since the 2022 truce allowed the Huthis to strengthen and improve their strategy and acquire even more sophisticated weaponry. Their intervention against Israel between late 2023 and 2025 gave them an international popularity boost. Links and support from Hezbollah and Iran contributed to their military skills, assisted by the purchase of advanced technological elements on the international market. They have also benefited from AI advances, as was demonstrated recently by their attempted use of Anthropic’s Claude to develop a missile and then to identify the cause of its failure. The Huthis have long since demonstrated the absurdity of dismissing their movement as a bunch of wild, sandal-wearing tribesmen armed with handguns. Partly as a consequence of the military battering suffered in 2025 from the fifty-two-day US bombing campaign and a number of well-targeted Israeli air strikes, Ansar Allah initially chose to stay on the sidelines of the US-Israeli war against Iran. It expressed support for Iran but only launched a few missiles against Israel in late March, thus maintaining the image of being anti-Israeli rather than pro-Iran. It is only since the breakdown of the “Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding” in late June that the Huthis have taken an active role in the Red Sea. Instead of closing the Bab al-Mandab Strait altogether, following Iranian statements that this option was an additional weapon in the struggle to control the world hydrocarbon market, the Huthis limited their blockade to Saudi shipping. They made a mutual nonaggression deal with the United States , stating that they would not interfere with shipping from any other country. One should note that this implies Israeli shipping is also welcome to use the Red Sea, contrary to the Huthi basic slogan “Death to America, Death to Israel!” and raising questions about their ideological commitments. Between March and July, the Saudis had transferred most of their oil exports through the East–West Pipeline to reach the sea, thus minimizing the disruption to their trade resulting from the Gulf blockades. Attacks on Saudi shipping in August reduced the amount of oil exported from Saudi Arabia’s Yanbu port from five million barrels per day to fewer than two million. This was in addition to the considerable additional cost and time needed to reach the East Asian market, as oil has to be transported all the way around Africa. This has contributed to the world oil crisis. The Huthi Offensives The Huthis had a number of reasons to initiate the fighting at this time. The twenty million people under their rule are suffering worsening poverty due to the growing economic impact of the US designation of Ansar Allah as a “foreign terrorist organization.” This has been combined with the almost complete withdrawal of humanitarian aid to Huthi-ruled areas. Although popular suffering is not a major motivation for Ansar Allah, poverty reduces potential sources of taxation, which is needed to finance military salaries and the purchase of weaponry. The closer relationship of Saudi Arabia with the IRG that followed the exclusion of Emirati-backed southern separatists in early 2026 was also an emerging threat. This was linked to efforts to overcome the remaining divisions within IRG-linked forces. Internationally, the Huthis were concerned about Saudi Arabia’s nascent initiatives, such as the Mecca Defence Alliance with Pakistan and Turkey and the Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition. The latter is a defensive naval alliance formed in July 2026 to protect shipping, international trade, and energy supply lines from Huthi attacks. The international situation will also have encouraged Huthi leaders, suggesting to them that neither the United States nor Israel was likely to focus on Yemen or Saudi Arabia while preoccupied with forthcoming elections and their ongoing, stalemated wars. Combined with a widespread sense of exhaustion over the “no war, no peace” situation, this will have motivated the Huthis to go on the attack while they were still clearly the stronger military entity. In July, the Saudis bombed the runway of Sana’a airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing. Ansar Allah used this as a pretext to justify escalation. It demanded an end to all blockades on Yemen and described Saudi Arabia as its main enemy, reviving the decade-old discourse and barely mentioning its Yemeni opponents. Starting in August, the offensive rapidly shifted from the better-defended Marib region, where the Huthis had failed to break through prior to the truce, to the southern Red Sea coast. Their rapid successes here made it possible to take Mokha and reach the Bab al-Mandab Strait and its islands by September 10. Although fighting persists in Marib and Saada, the main focus is now Taiz governorate and its capital, which is under siege and suffering both military and humanitarian emergencies. While conditions in Taiz are extreme, the city reflects a wider pattern of IRG fragmentation and offers the best site from which to examine Yemen’s political divisions. Taiz has been the focus of fighting between the Huthis and their opponents throughout the decade, with parts of the city and governorate under the control of either side. Long considered the country’s intellectual capital, it is home to the strongest elements of all political forces, from Salafis at one extreme to the Yemeni Socialist Party at the other, as well as a multiplicity of armed groups. As well as resisting the Huthis for the past decade, these forces have also fought against each other. At different times, military groups connected with al-Qaeda, the Islah party, Tareq Saleh’s National Resistance forces, and other elements have fought for control of the city and its sources of income. Today, in the face of a possible complete takeover by the Huthis, their opponents face an urgent need to overcome these differences. The IRG’s Weaknesses The rapid failure of Saudi-backed IRG forces in September came as a shock. Lack of coordination into a single effective command and rivalries between units demonstrated that the process of military restructuring that had been implemented since February was far from complete. As elsewhere in Yemen, patience was running thin with the “no war, no peace” situation, and the IRG was getting ready for the resumption of fighting. In response to the Huthi offensive, it launched the “Dawn of Yemen” counteroffensive in early October. This move successfully recovered some territory in the vicinity of the strait, but it has stalled without being able to break the siege of Taiz, despite some gains in the far north. There is no doubt that the IRG seriously underestimated Huthi technological capacities, and it may also have failed to develop its own skills in that sector. The absence of ground-based cadres certainly contributes to strategic failures, such as the one that resulted in the massacre of seventy-three new recruits and the wounding of more than two hundred in Shabwa on October 19. The “Dawn of Yemen” offensive aims to defeat the Huthis. To achieve that task, it would require unity, a sophisticated overall perspective, and preparations for a long-term struggle. Yemenis throughout the country desperately long for an end to the war with a reasonable agreement that would allow them to focus on recovery and development. The IRG is not the Saudi mercenary force that the Huthis speak of in their propaganda. But it cannot win the war on its own for both financial and political reasons, so it needs Saudi backing. Unfortunately, Saudi political influence remains a fundamental feature of the scene in Yemen that we cannot ignore. Saudi Dilemmas Ansar Allah has also been launching missile attacks on Saudi Arabia that are regular and often lethal. This has had a considerable impact on the Saudi economy. The latest highly publicized international event to have been postponed to better days was the annual “Davos in the Desert” investment conference. This followed a series of less prominent cancellations, all of which have affected the regime’s reputation and its ability to attract investment. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman must bitterly regret his initial decision to go to war against the Huthis in 2015 and has been trying to extricate his country from the Yemen quagmire since 2020. Negotiators were close to reaching a deal in late 2023, but the Gaza genocide and the US-Israeli war against Iran put paid to those efforts. While Iran is unlikely to be directly responsible for Huthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the contribution of those attacks to pressure on world hydrocarbon supplies helps Tehran in its stand-off with the United States. In the long run, Saudi vulnerability also weakens its potential for regional domination. The kingdom’s malaise has revealed the failure of the massive bribes it has dispensed over the course of decades to buy support in its hour of need. In spite of the recent international agreements, the rulers of Egypt and Pakistan are only offering limited assistance. British and French contributions will not change the course of the war, and the billions Riyadh has promised to Trump have not persuaded Washington to throw its weight on the scales. Having spent billions more on high-tech weaponry, mostly from the United States, the Saudi military finds itself unable to stop Huthi missiles, due to a lack of interceptors and the vastness of their country. Saudi Arabia now stands alone, facing the Huthis directly within its borders. Saudi Arabia’s experience since 2015 has confirmed that air strikes alone do not win a war. This has certainly contributed to the regime’s hesitation about deploying its military in Yemen once again — a military that already has a reputation as a “parade” force. But the IRG ground forces will need aerial support if they are going to reverse the Huthi gains of recent months. Huthi calls for major financial and political concessions from the Saudi regime become more and more unrealistic as they continue their strikes on Saudi infrastructure, raising the issue of Ansar Allah’s objectives. The dilemma for the Saudi regime worsens by the day: if it wants to reach a deal with the Huthis, that will require unacceptable and unfeasible concessions, but if it continues launching air strikes against their forces in Yemen, there will be more retaliation against targets within the kingdom. It is difficult to see Iran’s offer to mediate with the Huthis as anything other than an attempt to persuade the Saudis to make major concessions. Quiet mediation by Oman is also unlikely to achieve much while the Huthis believe they are on a winning streak. Meanwhile, millions of Yemenis are now in a state of deepening crisis, with hunger and the lack of medical supplies compounded by the risk of bombing, and without any end or hope in sight.
