articles.title: Milwaukee’s Proud History of Baseball — and Socialism
articles.author: Peter Dreier
articles.content: Organizers like to say that all politics boils down to a battle between organized money and organized people. Candidates with the largest war chests tend to win, but contenders who refuse to take donations from corporate interests can prevail if their supporters are well-organized, inspired, and strategic. Likewise, big employers can spend huge sums on union busting, but employees can win union organizing drives if they know how to mobilize workers to stick together and not be intimidated. The same is true in baseball. Teams in big markets with large payrolls have a decided advantage when it comes to recruiting talented players who command huge salaries, but feisty, scrappy teams with fewer stars can sometimes win championships. Since 2000, more than 80 percent of the teams that have advanced to the World Series ranked in the top half of league payrolls. Teams with the five largest payrolls (out of thirty teams) account for roughly 38 percent of all World Series contestants and nearly half (48 percent) of all World Series champions. But this year is an exception: the World Series contestants — the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays — are both among the poorer teams in baseball. Milwaukee is Major League Baseball’s smallest market in terms of population size and TV audience and ranks nineteenth in payroll ($143.5 million). Tampa Bay is twenty-fifth in market size and ranks twenty-sixth in payroll ($98.3 million). The top-spending teams are the New York Mets ($346.8 million) and the Los Angeles Dodgers ($338 million). Despite the disparity, the Brewers swept the Dodgers in four games in the National League Championship Series to make it to the World Series, thwarting LA’s hopes to win three consecutive World Series. The Brewers and Rays won their respective leagues by combining strong pitching, agile and savvy “small ball” play, and because of managers who utilized their rosters to get the most out of teams without many highly paid superstars. During the first half of the twentieth century, in both politics and baseball, Milwaukee’s have-nots often beat the odds. And indeed, those two histories are intertwined in ways not often appreciated. Milwaukee’s Sewer Socialists In the early 1900s, Milwaukee’s socialists came to power by forging an alliance with the city’s labor movement. The city’s culture was heavily shaped by German immigrants, whose athletic and gymnastic clubs embedded the ideal of a “sound mind in a sound body.” One of them, Turner Hall, built in 1883 near the city’s downtown, served as a gathering place for Milwaukee’s radicals and socialists. It provided its members a place to socialize, listen to music, drink beer, and discuss politics. Eugene Debs gave his first speech as a Socialist there in 1898 and spoke at Turner Hall on many other occasions. (It remains a popular site for meetings and performances, with a gym in the basement.) One of Turner Hall’s members was Victor Berger, an Austrian Jewish immigrant who spearheaded the Socialist Party’s rise to local power. Berger was a schoolteacher, an editor of two newspapers (one in German, another in English), and a skilled organizer. He and Debs helped found the Socialist Party of America (SP) in 1901. Berger built the Milwaukee branch into a formidable political machine. He secured the backing of the unions, including the powerful brewery workers’ locals and most German and Polish immigrants. The SP sponsored carnivals, picnics, singing societies, and even Sunday schools, conducting their campaigns in English, German, and Polish. In 1910, Milwaukee voters sent Berger to Washington as the country’s first socialist congressman. He lost his seat in 1912 but was elected again in 1918 and in a 1919 special election; both times the House refused to seat him because of his opposition to World War I. He returned to Congress in 1922, served three terms, and lost his seat in 1928. Berger sponsored bills for old-age pensions, government ownership of the radio industry, abolition of child labor, self-government for the District of Columbia, and a system of public works to provide relief for the unemployed. He also sponsored resolutions to withdraw federal troops from the Mexican border, for the abolition of the Senate (which was then not yet elected directly by the voters and was nicknamed the “millionaires’ club”), for women’s suffrage, and for federal ownership of the railroads. While none of Berger’s proposals gained much traction in Congress, his comrades in Milwaukee were a dominant force in the city’s civic life. In 1912, some 1,200 SP members held public office in 340 cities and towns across the United States, including Socialist mayors in Schenectady and Berkeley; Socialists would later win the mayor’s office in Minneapolis (1916) and Reading (1927). But Socialists’ most enduring success emerged in Milwaukee. Between 1910 and 1960, Milwaukee was led for nearly forty years by three Socialist mayors — Emil Seidel (1910–12), Daniel Hoan (1916–1940), and Frank Zeidler (1948–1960) — and also boasted a number of city council and school board members. “The workers of our city are its most valuable asset,” Seidel, a woodcarver and union leader, said in his inaugural address. During his two-year term, the city adopted an eight-hour day for municipal employees and increased their minimum wage from $1.75 to $2.00 a day. In 1910, the city added chlorine to the lake water, which sharply reduced the incidence of typhoid. A few years later, following a huge outbreak of diarrhea, the city stopped mixing raw sewage with drinking water. Milwaukee Mayor Daniel Hoan, circa 1930 ( San Francisco Examiner / CC BY 4.0 ) Opposed by Milwaukee’s business establishment, Seidel lost the 1912 election. That year he was the SP’s vice-presidential candidate, running alongside Debs. They gained 6 percent of the national vote, 8.4 percent in Wisconsin, and 27 percent in Milwaukee County. In 1916, the Milwaukee Socialists made a dramatic comeback, catapulting city attorney Daniel Webster Hoan into office. Hoan served as mayor until 1940. Detractors initially mocked them as “sewer socialists,” because they focused heavily on solving practical problems, not on revolutionary Marxist ideas. In 1936, Time magazine put Hoan on its cover and praised Milwaukee as “one of the best-run cities in the U.S.” Milwaukee’s voters kept reelecting Hoan because he ran efficient and humane administrations, showing it was possible to both expand public services and balance the city’s budget. The socialists expanded public education for the city’s working-class children (including free textbooks, lunches, and dental and medical programs), created an adult education program for workers, expanded the public libraries and playgrounds, and improved teachers’ salaries. In 1923, Socialist Charles Whitnall — a onetime city treasurer and founder of the Commonwealth Mutual Savings Bank for workers — created a master plan for a network of beautiful parks and protected the city’s Lake Michigan lakefront from development, to ensure the working class would have access to the beaches and other recreation areas. As a result, Milwaukee had the nation’s best municipal park system. In 1923, the Socialists built the country’s first city-sponsored public housing project, Garden Homes. They inaugurated a public bus system to replace the street trolleys that ran down the middle of the road, causing accidents and injuring pedestrians. Under Hoan, the Socialists adopted tough factory and building regulations and inspections, reined in police brutality against striking workers, improved working conditions for rank-and-file cops, and sponsored public markets. They gave preference to union shops for city contracts for everything from printing to horseshoeing. Hoan pushed for a law that allowed the mayor to close any factory if the employer refused to negotiate with the workers. The Socialists forced the city’s private streetcar company to pave the streets, lower fares, improve service, and pay fees to the city in exchange for its monopoly. They opened a municipal quarry to provide crushed rock for street projects, built a municipally owned water system, and created a pioneering sanitation infrastructure. In 1925, the city built the Jones Island water treatment plant, one of the first facilities of its kind, and still in operation. From the start, Milwaukee recycled its sewage sludge as Milorganite (for Mil waukee Org anic Nit rog e n), a fertilizer used on parks, golf courses, and lawns around the country. The treatment plant is now run by the Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District . It sells about 47,000 tons of Milorganite each year, which generates over $12 million in annual revenue for the city, turning a waste management cost into a major revenue stream. In 1932, voters elected Socialist labor lawyer Max Raskin — great-uncle of Jamie Raskin, currently a progressive congressman from Maryland — as city attorney. A close Hoan ally, Raskin was attacked by a conservative newspaper for refusing to prosecute “communistic rioters” — meaning strikers and protesters. Raskin required his assistant city attorneys to end any employment in private practice, which had been a source of corruption and conflicts of interest. Zeidler, the third Socialist mayor, was elected in 1948. He was a popular figure who shared the progressive values of his socialist predecessors, but by then the business community had gained greater influence; at least one major employer threatened to fire employees who voted for Zeidler. During his twelve years as mayor, the city doubled its geographic size by annexing nearby areas. In 1957, Fortune magazine called Milwaukee one of the two best-governed large cities in the country. During his time as mayor, Milwaukee’s black population nearly tripled, reaching 8 percent of the population by 1960. Among other measures, Zeidler pushed for the construction of racially integrated public housing. His political enemies tried to use his strong support for the civil rights movement against him, including spreading false rumors that he had erected billboards in the South urging African Americans to move to Milwaukee to take advantage of its liberal welfare programs. Business Ascends, Milwaukee Declines After Zeidler left office, the city was governed by several business-friendly mayors, which coincided with the city’s dramatic decline starting in the 1960s, from the eleventh to the thirty-first largest city in the country. Its population dropped from 741,000 people in 1960 to about 562,000 today, 23 percent of whom live below the poverty line. Banks fostered white flight to the suburbs by redlining Milwaukee’s neighborhoods. Today the Milwaukee area is one of the most racially segregated regions in the country. Milwaukee’s economy has never recovered from the massive job and population decline. A. O. Smith, the giant manufacturer of water heaters, boilers, and car frames, founded in 1874, still has its global headquarters in Milwaukee, but its production plants are now located in the American South as well as China, Mexico, India, and Turkey. Almost eight thousand union employees once worked at its factory on the city’s northwest side. After being abandoned for many years, the site is now an industrial park, but the number of employees is a small fraction of the former A. O. Smith workforce. Milwaukee was once home to brewery giants like Pabst, Schlitz (which promoted itself as “the beer that made Milwaukee famous”), Blatz, and Miller. In 1905, Milwaukee had 3,809 brewery workers in just eight major companies. It reached its peak in 1953, when Milwaukee had over 7,100 unionized brewery workers. Today a conglomerate called Molson Coors dominates the local beer industry. It employs about 1,200 people in Milwaukee in its main Miller brewery and its corporate offices. Many local draft breweries dot the area, but they produce a relatively small volume per worker compared to the large factories that once called Milwaukee home. Bill Veeck, Baseball’s Radical Owner Milwaukee’s working class embraced baseball as well as socialism. The city was home to minor league, employer-sponsored, semi-pro, and amateur teams. It was a hotbed for talent, particularly during the first half of the twentieth century. Since 1900, at least sixty-three Milwaukee natives have played in the majors, including such stars as Al Simmons (originally Aloysius Szymanski) and Tony Kubek (both of Polish descent) and Ken Keltner and Harvey Kuenn (both from blue-collar families of German ancestry). About another two hundred major leaguers have come from the rest of Wisconsin. Bill Veeck, pictured in 1944 while recovering from injuries sustained in World War II (US Marine Corps) Starting in 1878, Milwaukee sponsored several teams in the early days of professional baseball, none of which lasted for more than a few years. Teams called the Brewers participated in the Western Association from 1888 to 1891, the American Association in 1891, the Western League from 1892 to 1899, and the American League in 1900 and 1901. The longest-lasting franchise, from 1902 to 1952, was the Brewers team in the top-level minor league, the American Association. The Brewers, as well as the Negro National League’s Milwaukee Bears (1923) and the Milwaukee Chicks of the All American Girls Professional Baseball League (1944), played at the quirky, wooden Borchert Field, a privately owned stadium on the city’s North Side. Built in 1888 to accommodate five thousand spectators, its capacity grew to eighteen thousand after several expansions. Ironically, baseball’s greatest maverick, Bill Veeck, then only twenty-seven, purchased the bankrupt, last-place minor-league Brewers in 1941, the year after Hoan was defeated for reelection. Born in 1914, Veeck grew up in baseball. His father was a sportswriter who wound up as president of the Chicago Cubs. He dropped out of college after his father died and did odd jobs for the Cubs. He had an unusual appreciation (for a white fan) for Negro League players. He put together a syndicate of investors to buy the Brewers, a struggling Triple-A team in the American Association. He was the last owner to purchase a baseball franchise without an independent fortune. During his five seasons as Brewers owner, Veeck revolutionized the game. Veeck was both a shrewd businessman and a radical reformer. He voted for perennial Socialist Party presidential candidate Norman Thomas even after Thomas had died. “I’d rather vote for a dead man with class than two live bums,” he later said. Veeck loved to sit in the bleachers and hang out with the working-class fans. He packed Borchert Field during World War II by scheduling Brewers’ games in the morning so that workers on the late shift at war plants could attend games. He also served a breakfast of cornflakes at the game. He staged free days for cab drivers and bartenders. In Milwaukee, Veeck began giving away promotion prizes — caps, a keg of nails, bottles of soda, pizza, and even animals (turkeys, geese, pigs, lobsters, and rabbits) — to attract fans to the park. Veeck modernized and cleaned the stadium’s restrooms specifically to make the ballpark more welcoming to female fans, a vastly underserved market at the time. He gave away orchids to women fans on Mother’s Day. He staged weddings at home plate. Satchel Paige in 1947 (ACME Newspictures) Sportswriters dubbed him “the [P. T.] Barnum of Baseball.” But he wasn’t just a showman. Despite a shoestring budget, he took the Brewers from last place in 1941 to a second-place finish in 1942, followed by three consecutive American Association pennants from 1943 to 1945; the Brewers’ attendance shattered minor league records. Veeck used similar promotional strategies when he purchased the Cleveland Indians in 1946. He owned the St Louis Browns (1951–53) and bought the Chicago White Sox (1959–1961, 1975–1981). Throughout his life, Veeck was an ardent anti-racist. When he purchased the Brewers, he inherited the team’s spring training facility in Ocala, Florida. During one game, Veeck decided to sit in the “colored” section of the stands. The local police showed up, told him he couldn’t sit there, and ordered him to move, threatening to arrest him for violating Florida’s Jim Crow laws. He told the town’s mayor that he’d move the team’s lucrative spring training program out of Ocala if they arrested him. They didn’t, but he moved the Brewers anyway. In 1947, Veeck’s Cleveland Indians hired Larry Doby, the first black player in the American League. The next year, he made Negro League star Satchel Paige, then forty-two-years old, the first black pitcher in the league. That team won the 1948 World Series. He joined the local NAACP and appeared, along with Doby and Paige, on a poster designed to recruit new members to the civil rights organization, featuring the phrase, “The NAACP gets the ball for you.” When he owned the White Sox, he canceled the team’s spring training reservations at Miami’s McAllister Hotel when it refused to accommodate black players, moving the entire team to another hotel. In 1970, he testified in federal court on behalf of Cardinals’ African American outfielder Curt Flood, who was suing major league baseball to overturn the reserve clause, baseball’s version of indentured servitude. Veeck expressed his socialist views when it came to baseball’s business side, too. At meetings of owners and in public statements, Veeck argued that wealthy teams in big markets should share revenue with teams in small markets to level the playing field and create a competitive balance. He contended that when his lowly St Louis Browns played the prosperous New York Yankees, they were entitled to a 50 percent share of the Yankees’ local television revenue, observing, “We’re half the show. They can’t play the game without us.” The other owners hated Veeck and his ideas. Boston Red Sox owner Tom Yawkey called Veeck “that damned socialist.” Corporatization Comes for Baseball After Veeck sold the Brewers, the team stayed in Milwaukee as a minor league franchise. In the late 1940s, the corporate-backed Greater Milwaukee Committee pushed for construction of a new publicly funded stadium with the explicit goal of attracting a major league franchise to the city. Their plan had some elements of the socialists’ focus on public works and recreational infrastructure, but it was hardly on behalf of the city’s working class. County Stadium opened in April 1953 as the first major ballpark in the United States financed entirely with public funds. The new ballpark enticed the Boston Braves to Milwaukee. In 1952, the minor league Brewers had attracted 195,839 fans to Borchert Field. The following season, the Braves lured 1.8 million fans to County Stadium. To increase revenue, the stadium was also used for Green Bay Packers football games, religious services, concerts, ice skating, and other large events. In 1957, the Braves, with stars like Hank Aaron, Warren Spahn, and Eddie Mathews, won the National League pennant and defeated the Yankees in the World Series. That season, attendance at County Stadium reached 2.2 million, first among the sixteen major league teams. The next season, the Braves again faced the Yankees in the World Series but lost four out of seven games. The team’s on-field performance and attendance declined steadily after that. In 1965, only 555,584 fans showed up, as the Braves slipped to fifth place in the National League, while Milwaukee suffered from the loss of jobs and population. The following year, the team moved to Atlanta. In 1970, as part of MLB expansion, car dealer Bud Selig brought together a group of investors and persuaded the other owners to approve another major league team in Milwaukee. He purchased the bankrupt Seattle Pilots, moved them to Milwaukee, and named the new team the Brewers after the minor league team he grew up watching. The Milwaukee Braves play at County Stadium in September 1960. (Robert Jahnke / CC BY 2.0 ) Starting in the late 1980s, Selig threatened to move the team out of Milwaukee if the state government didn’t build a modern, retractable-roof stadium. He claimed that the aging County Stadium couldn’t generate the revenue need to keep the team competitive, such as sales of luxury suites. In 1995, with the support of local business leaders, the politicians complied, enacting a 0.1 percent regional sales tax across five Wisconsin counties, in addition to funds from the state, county, and city. Like its predecessor, the new stadium was built with public funds. Although business and civic leaders called it a public-private partnership, it was little more than crony capitalism. Taxpayers paid for the stadium but, under the lease agreement, didn’t share in the Brewers’ profits. The public paid $609 million to pay off the building costs, borrowing interest, and maintenance. The Milwaukee-based Lynde and Harry Bradley Foundation, known as a right-wing philanthropy, provided a $20 million loan. The Brewers’ contribution was less than $40 million, almost all of it from the Miller Brewing Company, which paid the team that amount for naming rights. As a result, the stadium was called Miller Park from its opening in 2001 until the conclusion of the 2020 season. Despite investing so little in the ballpark, the Brewers own 36 percent of the facility, while the state-created Southeast Wisconsin Professional Baseball Park District owns the rest. In 1998, Selig’s fellow owners named him baseball commissioner, and he put his financial stake in the team in a trust managed by his daughter Wendy. The family sold the Brewers in 2005 to Los Angeles investor Mark Attanasio, who still owns the team. Twenty-two of Major League Baseball’s stadiums currently have corporate naming rights deals. In 2020, the Brewers switched their ballpark’s name from a brewery company’s to that of an insurance corporation. American Family Insurance, ranked 226 on the Fortune 500 list, with $19.6 billion in revenues, signed a fifteen-year agreement to pay about $4 million a year to change the stadium name to American Family Field. Milwaukee’s early socialists would certainly be outraged that even though the stadium is publicly owned, the Brewers control corporate sponsorships and stadium naming rights and have used their political clout to block efforts to get the legislature to split sponsorship revenues equally between the team and the state. If the socialists still ran the city, or if Bill Veeck still owned the team, the Brewers might be playing in Victor Berger Field or Daniel Hoan Stadium. Miller Park, now American Family Field, in 2005 (Jeramey Jannene / CC BY 2.0 ) In 2023, the Brewers persuaded Wisconsin lawmakers to subsidize renovations of American Family Field for around $500 million. Ryan Clancy, a Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member who serves in the Wisconsin State Legislature and was previously a member of the Milwaukee County Board of Supervisors, was an outspoken opponent of using public funds for stadium renovations, which he calls “corporate socialism” and “corporate welfare.” Clancy thinks tax revenues should focus on local services such as public transit, parks, public safety, and housing, rather than subsidizing Attanasio’s team. Attanasio paid $223 million to buy the Brewers in 2005; by 2016, the franchise was worth $875 million. Today the team is worth $1.9 billion, according to Forbes . Baseball has been totally corporatized since Bill Veeck’s day. His entire career was devoted to baseball, and he was always in financial distress. In contrast, Attanasio, the latest Brewers’ owner, made his initial fortune with the private equity firm Crescent Capital Group. He not only owns the Brewers but is also majority shareholder of English football club Norwich City and part-owner of the American Hockey League’s Milwaukee Admirals. He is also on the board of directors for LA28, which oversees plans for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles. Although he’s hardly a progressive, much less a socialist, he is one of the few baseball owners who primarily contributes to Democratic candidates. Although he has a net worth of $1.9 billion, Attanasio is among the poorest of the thirty MLB team owners. The wealthiest is Mets owner Steve Cohen, a Wall Street hedge fund tycoon with a net worth of $22 billion. Second is Edward Rogers III, who owns the Toronto Blue Jays and is worth $11 billion, according to Forbes . He inherited the telecommunications and media empire founded by his father, which includes Rogers Wireless, Rogers Cable (Canada’s largest cable TV provider), forty-six radio stations, seventy consumer and trade magazines, and the Blue Jays. Mark Walter, the Dodgers’ largest shareholder, ranks third, with an estimated net worth between $7 billion and $13 billion. Walter is cofounder and CEO of the financial conglomerate Guggenheim Partners. Last year, he bought a majority stake in the Los Angeles Lakers basketball team and sold it just fourteen months later to former Disney CEO Bob Iger and Thrive Capital founder Joshua Kushner (Jared’s younger brother) at a $12.5 billion valuation — $2.5 billion more than the team was valued at when he bought it. Walter is also co-owner of the WNBA’s Los Angeles Sparks and is a major investor in England’s Chelsea football club. The Brewers didn’t win their first pennant until 1982, when they played in the American League, and lost to the St Louis Cardinals in a seven-game World Series. The team shifted to the National League in 1998. It finally won another pennant this year, leading the majors with 103 wins. Out of Left Field Debates over socialism are now shaking up both baseball and politics. By 1993, the revenue and payroll disparities in the MLB had become untenable. The small-market franchises were struggling to keep up with escalating player salaries in larger markets: the Yankees’ television and radio income was $47 million, while the Brewer’s collected only $5.5 million. It wasn’t until the 1990s — following a strike by the Major League Baseball Players Association (MLBPA) — that baseball’s moguls adopted a version of Veeck’s decades-old revenue-sharing plan (although without giving him credit). Yankees owner George Steinbrenner was one of those who fiercely resisted any proposal to redistribute revenue. “I’m a charitable guy,” he said. “But I don’t like the idea of a socialist state. The Yankees shouldn’t be punished for their success.” In January 1994, the owners approved a plan to pool local broadcasting and gate revenues to aid small-market clubs. But they made their plan contingent on the players’ union agreeing to a salary cap. The MLBPA rejected the deal, which it saw as a way to suppress player earnings and restrict the free-agent market. The owners rebuffed the union’s counterproposal, which included a luxury tax on the sixteen highest-payroll teams and putting 25 percent of all gate receipts into a pool that would be shared with the lowest-payroll teams. The impasse led to a 232-day strike that canceled the 1994 World Series. It only ended in 1995 when federal judge Sonia Sotomayor (now a US Supreme Court justice) issued an injunction against the owners. The collective bargaining agreement, finalized in 1997, severed revenue sharing from the idea of a salary cap. Under that landmark agreement, wealthy, large-market clubs transferred a portion of their local revenues to small-market teams, and a luxury tax was placed on high-spending teams to fund the revenue-sharing pool meant to level the playing field. Despite these reforms, there’s still a wide gap in revenue and payroll between the thirty teams. Both the NFL and NBA have much more progressive formulas for leveling the playing field. MLB rules don’t require teams to spend their additional revenue on payroll. On average, teams spend about half their total revenue on salaries, but the range is dramatic. The Mets allocate about 90 percent of their revenue on player salaries, for instance, while the Marlins spend only 26 percent of their $317 million revenue on payroll. Fans in some small markets have accused their teams of treating revenue-sharing as a profit center, not as a way to create a competitive balance. The Brewers are the most generous spenders among small-market teams, investing 41 percent of revenue into player salaries. But the small-market teams have a hard time retaining their best players because they can’t match the salary offers of the wealthier teams. The most expensive players are not going to play in Milwaukee, Pittsburgh, Miami, or Tampa Bay. Baseball’s owners and the union are currently in the middle of negotiations over the next collective bargaining agreement. Under current Commissioner Rob Manfred, the owners are more adamant than ever that the union must agree to a salary cap. Close observers believe that it could lead the owners to initiate a lockout. Many fans view baseball’s labor-management battles as a conflict between billionaires and millionaires. Twenty-seven of baseball’s thirty owners are billionaires. Only Colorado Rockies owner Dick Monfort (worth a mere $700 million), Miami Marlins owner Bruce Sherman ($500 million), and Cincinnati Reds owner Bob Castellini ($400 million) fall below the threshold. Meanwhile, thanks to the players’ union and the end of the reserve clause in the 1970s, players’ salaries and working conditions have improved dramatically. The average player salary is $5.34 million, but this is heavily skewed by a small number of star players with enormous contracts. The median salary — $1.4 million — provides a more realistic picture. But even that figure is misleading, because the typical major league career is only five years. Most players are only short-term millionaires. Attendance at major league games this season reached 71.7 million, close to the highest on record. The thirty teams generated $12 billion in revenue this year, the second highest amount in the sport’s history. The typical cost for a family of four to attend a major league game ranges from $159 for the Miami Marlins to $413 at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles. In most major league ballparks, the workers who clean the stadiums, sell the food and concessions, and work in the parking lots are unionized with UNITE HERE or SEIU, but these are seasonal jobs and many of the employees have a hard time making ends meet. Baseball’s owners can afford to reduce the price of tickets, parking, and concessions for fans, and improve wages for stadium employees, without placing a cap on player salaries. The cost of attending baseball games is part of the nation’s affordability crisis, itself a symptom of the widening gaps in wealth and income. It is one reason why socialism is gaining traction. Polls show growing support for socialism over capitalism, while the number of socialists elected to office is skyrocketing. Membership in DSA reached over 120,000 this year, a huge increase in just a decade. These trends are reflected in Milwaukee. The local DSA chapter has grown from 350 members in 2025 to about one thousand today. (Madison, the state capital and home to the University of Wisconsin, has a similar number of members.) The dramatic spurt in members across the state made it possible for Francesca Hong , one of four DSAers in the state legislature, to come close to winning the Democratic nomination for governor this year. Alex Brower, a thirty-nine-year old DSA member and former union organizer, was elected to Milwaukee’s city council in 2025. He grew up in Wisconsin and is a stalwart Brewers fan. He is thrilled that his team will be in the current World Series. But he also views Major League Baseball as a big business that cares more about its profits than the lives of its customers (the fans) or its working-class employees. The Milwaukee DSA chapter has been waging campaigns to municipalize the city’s private utility, restrict the repressive forces of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, protect tenants from unscrupulous landlords, and support workers’ union drives. Brower would eventually like to see DSA and its allies wage a campaign to bring the Brewers under public or community control, similar to the arrangement that governs the nearby Green Bay Packers . Even though a government agency owns American Family Field, “the Brewers get all the benefits and the community gets nothing,” said Brower. He noted that zip code 53206, which is just a few miles from the stadium, is one of the poorest areas in the state. “The Brewer’s merch is flying off the shelves,” he said, while some of the poorest Milwaukeeans are paying a sales tax to finance and fix up the ballpark. “The rest of us have to pick up the tab, including paying for the cops who direct traffic on game days, and the wear and tear on the streets.” “Milwaukee’s brewery workers were socialists,” Brower explained. “So shouldn’t the Milwaukee Brewers reflect that legacy?” Daniel Hoan couldn’t have said it better. articles.title: How American History Celebrates Enslavers and Erases Their Victims
articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Recently, a friend asked whether I had seen the documentary Natchez . Knowing of my involvement in Coming to the Table , he sent a link, encouraged me to watch, and asked whether I would write about it afterward. Coming to the Table brings together descendants of enslaved people and enslavers, along with others committed to racial justice, to uncover history, build relationships, pursue healing, and take action. Through that work, I have come to know Tom DeWolf, a founding member and longtime leader. His ancestors, the DeWolfs of Bristol, Rhode Island, were the largest slave-trading family in U.S. history, responsible for trafficking approximately 10,000 Africans into slavery. Tom joined nine relatives on a journey confronting that history, documented in Traces of the Trade: A Story from the Deep North and his book, Inheriting the Trade . His work asks whose suffering supplied a family’s wealth and what responsibilities follow from knowing that truth. Those questions shaped my viewing of Natchez . Watching it left me gutted. As a Black woman descended from enslaved people, I cannot separate this history from my ancestors’ lives. The persistent disregard for their pain hurts. Watching that disregard persist among people alive today adds another injury. Natchez exposes competing accounts of the plantation South. Black guides and preservationists challenge the mythology. The film’s willingness to expose it matters. What gutted me was the continuing appetite for the fantasy it documents. In 2026, there is still a market for plantation grandeur that keeps the people whose captivity sustained it at an emotional distance. Houses become treasures. Enslavers maintain the veneer of accomplished gentlemen. The people they brutalized are little more than background. A documentary needs an audience to be made and distributed. Audiences can seek confrontation with history or reassurance about it. Natchez brings those competing desires into view. My indictment is of the continuing acceptance and appetite for the antebellum myth: the desire to enjoy the beauty without fully facing its brutality and the human cost. I have encountered that desire intimately. Years ago, I dated a man who told me slavery was wrong but insisted we could not judge the Founders by today’s standards. I ended the relationship that day. His defense asked me to accommodate his admiration for the founders while accepting his emotional distance from hundreds of people they harmed and the generations descended from them. I could not build intimacy with someone whose admiration mattered more to him than my ancestors humanity. Enslaved people did not need today’s standards to understand the wrong being done to them. Their resistance, escapes, and testimony bore witness to their suffering at the hands of tormentors we continue to deify—and to their rejection of a system whose brutality admirers of enslavers still find ways to excuse. My ancestors’ suffering was historical. His unwillingness to take it seriously was happening then, to me, the Black woman standing before him. Consider how differently we recognize captivity elsewhere. In 1991, Phillip Garrido and his wife, Nancy, abducted eleven-year-old Jaycee Dugard. They held her captive for eighteen years. Beginning when Jaycee was 11 years old, Phillip repeatedly raped her; she gave birth at fourteen and seventeen. In Austria, Josef Fritzl imprisoned his eighteen-year-old daughter, Elisabeth, in a cellar for twenty-four years, repeatedly raping her. She bore seven children; one died in infancy. Both men were convicted and imprisoned. Garrido received 431 years to life; Fritzl received life imprisonment. Their crimes were recognized as horrific violations of human beings. Before their arrests, Garrido and Fritzl had careers. Garrido operated his own printing business. Fritzl was an electrical engineer and rental-property owner. Now imagine documentaries inviting us to admire Garrido’s entrepreneurship or Fritzl’s engineering accomplishments. Imagine mentioning their victims briefly before returning to the men’s achievements. Who would buy a ticket to see that? - The producers would be hard pressed to find a market that could stomach that distortion of the facts. Yet change the setting to a plantation, and the arrangement becomes familiar. The brutality required to hold hundreds of people captive recedes from the story. Admirers come for the gowns, the table settings, the grandeur. Imagine presenting Hitler’s home that way: inviting visitors to admire his taste while relegating his victims to the background. We would recognize the obscenity. Why does plantation nostalgia still find a willing audience in the United States? Harriet Jacobs, who escaped slavery and became an abolitionist, described her enslaver’s relentless sexual pursuit in her 1861 autobiography, Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl . She testified to the terror of girlhood under another person’s claimed ownership. Under hereditary slavery, children inherited their mother’s enslaved status. An enslaver could rape a woman and claim the resulting child—even his own child—as property to work, inherit, or sell. The resemblance to modern captivity is therefore substantive: control over bodies, labor, movement, and children. Legal cover enlarged the perpetrator’s power and wealth. It did nothing to diminish the victim’s suffering. Black men lived under that power, too. In his 1845 autobiography, Frederick Douglass described the violence and relentless labor imposed by Edward Covey: “I was broken in body, soul, and spirit.” Bloodied after a beating, he appealed to Thomas Auld, the man who claimed ownership of him. Auld sent him back, insisting Covey “was a good man.” That judgment echoes through our commemorations. How much cruelty can a celebrated man’s reputation absorb before admiration becomes indefensible? At Choctaw Hall, one of the mansions toured in the film, guide and co-owner David Garner recounts defending Southern gentlemen against an accusation of arrogance: “We’re just proud of what we accomplished.” He credits seven generations of hard work for the surroundings visitors see. Whose work? Who built, cooked, cleaned, cultivated, and served? Whose captivity generated wealth? Where are their names when family pride takes center stage? The market for this selective memory was cultivated. After the Civil War, the Lost Cause movement promoted honorable Confederates, benevolent enslavers, and faithful enslaved people. Monuments, entertainment, and commemorations carried those images into national life. Confederate defeat opened the possibility for another future. During Reconstruction, Black Americans voted, held office, and built institutions. But white supremacists successfully fought those gains through terror and political resistance. As a result, federal protection receded. The former Confederate insurrectionists regained power, established Jim Crow and the racialized terror of lynching. That outcome was made possible by political choices in both the North and the South. Popular culture helped sustain it by romanticizing the defeated Confederacy while marginalizing the people it fought to keep enslaved. The blockbuster success of Gone with the Wind reveals how eagerly audiences embraced that mythology. Germany’s reckoning with Nazism was neither immediate nor complete. Nevertheless, its eventual official culture of remembrance made acknowledgment of Nazi crimes a national responsibility. Not so in the United States which has continued to uphold admiration for enslavers by distancing them from the implications of historical truth. That protection has contemporary consequences. When exploitation disappears from the history of wealth, inherited advantage looks entirely earned. When imposed disadvantage disappears, racial inequality looks like Black failure. Demands for repair then look like requests for undeserved favors. The injury also reaches beyond money. We learn whose pain requires an explanation before it deserves concern. I believe that habit connects the minimization of enslaved people’s suffering to the excuses made for mistreating Black people today, including by law enforcement. Authority receives the benefit of the doubt. The injured person must establish innocence, compliance, or respectability before receiving empathy. What did he do? Why didn’t he comply? Was the officer afraid? These questions can shift attention away from whether the person exercising power acted justly. Historical defenses can perform a similar function: explaining the powerful while distancing us from those they harmed. No single cause explains unequal policing. But the danger is documented. A 2019 study found that Black men and women faced greater lifetime risks of being killed by police than their white counterparts. Research also shows that Black pain can be discounted. A 2016 study found that white medical students and residents who endorsed false beliefs about biological racial differences made less accurate assessments of Black patients’ pain and less accurate treatment recommendations. That study concerns medicine. It nevertheless demonstrates that assumptions about Black bodies can affect whether suffering receives an adequate response. The stories we circulate can challenge those assumptions or leave them comfortable and undisturbed. This is a public safety issue. Black people are part of the public. Our safety cannot be expendable in the pursuit of someone else’s sense of order. After George Floyd’s murder, Coming to the Table explicitly connected police violence with the responsibility to transform institutions sustaining white supremacy. That connection explains why I belong at the table. Truth-telling must lead to changes in conduct, policy, and accountability. Healing cannot mean asking injured people to make peace with everyone else’s comfort. When someone says slavery happened too long ago to matter, I wonder why that reasoning applies to the debt but never to the inheritance. The mansions of Natchez embody wealth created through uncompensated labor. Why is it too late to compensate the descendants of the people whose labor created that wealth, but never too late for others to inherit its benefits? And why, in 2026, does an audience still want a version of that history organized around the enslaver’s pride? That appetite is the indictment. Every generation decides what it will celebrate and whose suffering it will accommodate. Today’s indifference is another injury, inflicted by people who can choose differently. The friend who sent me Natchez asked what I thought. I’m left asking: Whose history are we preserving when the enslaver’s reputation receives more protection than his victims ever did—and whose safety are we compromising when we carry that same hierarchy of concern into the present? articles.title: Vancouver Is in the Middle of a Socialist Surge
articles.author: James Adair
articles.content: Vancouver’s contrasts are visible on its streets. Luxury cars cruise past some of North America’s worst homeless encampments. Last Saturday, October 17, the city produced a political contrast to match: after four years of a center-right city hall, its municipal council has transformed into one of the most left-wing in North America. The breakthrough comes alongside strong socialist showings in municipal elections around the world, from Zohran Mamdani’s win in New York to Die Linke’s recent state election victory in Berlin. The Coalition of Progressive Electors (COPE), a democratic socialist party, elected all twelve candidates it ran: four to council, four to school board, and four to park board. COPE’s Sean Orr topped the council ballot in raw votes. Together with the four Green councilors, OneCity’s sole council seat, and Green Mayor Pete Fry , COPE’s four council wins give the progressive bloc nine of ten councilor seats and the mayor’s office — ten of city hall’s eleven elected seats. As right-leaning candidates made gains in other British Columbia municipalities, and as the social democratic New Democratic Party fought to retain power in the October 24 provincial election, COPE’s result testified to the party’s hard work and organizing efforts. It vindicated a party that was presumed dead after its near wipeout four years ago. The Breach reported in depth on COPE’s lengthy effort to rebuild its membership and organizing capacity, give members a meaningful role in shaping the party, and embrace its socialist identity rather than blur it into generic progressivism. That work positioned COPE to capitalize on the growing working-class discontent and the material realities of everyday life in Vancouver. A City in Crisis Vancouver’s housing crisis formed the backdrop to COPE’s victory. More than half of the city’s households rent. In 2021, approximately 39 percent of renter households spent at least 30 percent of their income on shelter, while roughly one-quarter were in core housing need: their homes were unaffordable, unsuitable, or inadequate, and they could not afford acceptable alternatives. The problem extends beyond the poorest residents. Even relatively well-paid workers can struggle to find housing near their jobs, while homeownership is increasingly out of reach for younger people. Economic insecurity has become a defining feature of everyday life in the city. ABC Vancouver came to power promising to address the problem by speeding up approvals and building more housing. Its administration can point to real increases in housing approvals and rental development. But more construction hasn’t made Vancouver affordable for many of the people who need homes. In September 2026, a report found that more than five thousand completed condominiums across Metro Vancouver remained unsold, with an estimated value of $4.45 billion. The chasm between new housing and what people can afford was stark. Mayor Ken Sim’s city council also shuttered the Vancouver Renters Office, which provided resources and information on tenant rights and how to navigate the legal system. Homelessness also increased in Vancouver under ABC. In contrast, COPE’s platform called for the city to acquire existing apartment buildings and convert them into permanently affordable public housing and co-ops. It also proposed a tax on properties worth more than $5 million to fund efforts to end homelessness, tripling the Empty Homes Tax, as well as stronger tenant protections. It put housing and care at the center of its strategy to respond to the city’s interlocking problems. That emphasis was particularly significant in the Downtown Eastside, where COPE has historically maintained a strong base. The neighborhood has been at the center of Vancouver’s overlapping problems of poverty, housing insecurity, and drug poisoning. Its residents have endured these conditions through successive governments that have promised to restore order without providing the necessary housing and care. The Campaign On Election Day, volunteers reportedly knocked on more than ten thousand doors. The campaign gave voters a positive vision of the city, championing socialized housing, public grocers, and expanded public services like Wi-Fi, libraries, and washrooms. Its “Fight for Vancouver” platform set out a high-level road map. The slogan, “Evict Ken Sim,” aimed at the outgoing right-wing mayor, became a meme, appearing in art, on buttons dotting the city, and on campaign merch like T-shirts. COPE’s younger candidates, including Solomon Yi-Kieran , Vancouver’s youngest-ever city councilor, and Chloe Leslie, brought passion and vitality to the party’s communications. Rather than imitating Zohran Mamdani’s style, they drew on Vancouver’s own culture, making high-energy, often playful social media videos. The new council has an opportunity to reverse some of ABC’s policies and pursue shared progressive priorities. But a progressive majority is not the same thing as a socialist government, and the parties will not necessarily agree on how to use their power. COPE’s platform went much further than the Greens’ on important questions of public ownership and the role of municipal government. Its proposals for public acquisition of housing and taxes on high-value properties went beyond simply making private development easier. The question is how much of this agenda COPE can persuade its coalition partners to adopt. Will the new council commit to a more ambitious public housing program? Will it restore tenant protections and supportive-housing investments? Will it redirect resources toward public services? Just as important is how COPE will maintain its independent political identity while participating in a governing coalition. Building a movement from outside city hall can be easier than sustaining it once its representatives become responsible for budgets, compromises, and the day-to-day operations of government. Moving Forward COPE’s members now have to decide how to use their electoral mandate. They can negotiate for improvements inside the council while continuing to organize tenants, workers, and neighborhoods to demand more from the new administration. The two approaches can complement and strengthen one another: COPE’s ability to mobilize people outside city hall may determine how much it can achieve inside. The challenge will be to keep the routines of municipal government from displacing the organizing that made the victory possible. Sean Orr, first elected in a 2025 by-election, has demonstrated that he can be a serious legislator as well as an organizer; COPE’s new batch of councilors can draw on his experience as they orient themselves to the workings of city hall. The coalition also faces a profound public safety challenge. Ken Sim’s council majority put two nonbinding plebiscites on the ballot: one asked whether the city should toughen laws against open-air hard drug use in public spaces; the other asked whether the city should push the province to create a secure medical facility with voluntary as well as one-hundred-plus involuntary beds. Voters backed both questions by roughly 68 percent. COPE and the Greens opposed putting the question to a vote, but the results largely refute any claim that the new progressive majority has a clear mandate to counter these proposals. It is very likely that some of the same people who voted for COPE voted yes to the plebiscites. Vancouver has been at the center of Canada’s overdose crisis, and the incoming council will be responsible for addressing conflicting expectations about the best way to respond to visible street-level poverty, public drug use, and complex mental health and addiction challenges. COPE will have to demonstrate that an approach rooted in housing, harm reduction, and public services can address residents’ concerns without abandoning its commitments to the people most affected by the crisis. The election does not resolve these questions. It makes them more urgent. One part of COPE’s rebuild was reconnecting members with the party’s history. Organizers made a slideshow of its victories since its founding in the 1960s, giving members a sense of that history and purpose. From declaring Vancouver a nuclear-weapon-free zone to Sean Orr establishing an arts and culture land trust, COPE exists in a long line of struggles for better housing, care, and socialism in the city. On October 17, the members gathered in a packed auditorium had good reason to pop champagne bottles, sing, and celebrate. They had done something many thought impossible. Socialism was back in Vancouver. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: It’s the Rent, Actually
articles.content: Deanna Muz, a retired nurse living in Saginaw, Mich., has typically voted Republican. But with ​ “ the way our economy is and all the BS going on,” she says, ​ “ I’m in that ​ ‘ I’m not sure’ phase.” Chief among Muz’s economic concerns is her housing — specifically, the sale of her manufactured home community to the private equity firm Brookfield Asset Management, and the possibility that subsequent rent and fee increases will force her to leave. In other words, she’s the kind of voter Democrats might hope to woo with an appeal to affordability, the political watchword of the moment. But for millions of struggling renters, that appeal may still sound fuzzy, at best. In June, Congress passed the 21 st Century ROAD to Housing Act, major bipartisan legislation aimed at boosting housing supply through regulatory changes. But implementation could take years, especially given reductions to federal housing staff. And while increasing housing supply is important, ​ “ none of that is really materially relevant to people who are struggling to make rent next week or next month,” says Alex Jacquez, a senior vice president at the Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive economic think tank. Earlier this year, the group released polling showing that nearly two-thirds of likely voters say that reining in corporate landlords, not solely building more housing, is key to bringing down costs. The June housing law also restricted investor purchases of single-family homes — but not apartments or manufactured homes, to Muz’s disappointment. (The legislation did include reforms aimed at expanding future production and siting of manufactured homes.) Muz spent the spring advocating for Michigan legislation that would create new pathways for manufactured housing residents to purchase mobile home parks themselves when owners plan to sell. But the measures, championed by the grassroots group MHAction, are still pending. While she owns her home itself, Muz, like most park residents, must pay ​ “ lot rent” on the land underneath it. And since most so-called mobile homes are often expensive or impossible to move, acquiring parks and raising those rents is a profitable strategy for investors, one of whom infamously compared the venture to running a Waffle House ​ “ where everyone is chained to the booths.” Rents have already risen since the park was purchased by a different out-of-state firm a few years ago. ​ “ I don’t know where I’m going to be in two years if they keep doing what they’re doing,” Muz says. Abbie Pedrotte, a neighbor of Muz’s who votes Democrat, already pays $ 560 in lot rent ​ “ for nothing,” she says. She worries about falling behind, being evicted and losing her entire investment if she’s unable to move her home in time. Both Muz and Pedrotte name housing affordability as a top political issue for them — and the common ground between the two neighbors may be something of a national microcosm, according to Steven Kull, director of the University of Maryland’s Program for Public Consultation, which surveys the public on policy issues where there appears to be substantial common ground, despite gridlock in government. In July, Kull’s team published results from polling on housing affordability administered across 11 electorally competitive states and 28 competitive congressional districts, including the one encompassing Saginaw. The survey found strong support for key elements of the new federal housing law — including limiting corporate home-buying and stimulating private investment through tax credits — but also support for ​ “ policies that go substantially further,” Kull notes. For example, 86 % of Democrats and 64 % of Republicans said that they would back billions in direct investment to build housing affordable for low- and very low-income households. The takeaway, Kull says, is that dissatisfaction with the cost of living is driving ​ “ a remarkable level of support … for a much more activist government role.” Will an affordability agenda deliver on this demand for bolder action on housing? It depends on whose agenda. Democrats’ near unanimous embrace of the term followed the June 2025 primary victory of then mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani, who ran on freezing rents for more than 2 million rent-stabilized tenants. A year later, you’d be hard-pressed to find a politician or caucus that hasn’t released an affordability agenda, which might refer alternately to tax breaks, permitting reform, or sweeping new social programs funded by taxes on billionaires. Housing is central to the push and pull over the politics of affordability, as a new crop of left-wing congressional candidates run on freezing rents and protecting renters, building off the momentum of years of resurgent tenant organizing. From Pedrotte’s vantage point, it makes little sense to talk about affordability as an abstraction. ​ “ I think the conversation about affordable housing and the conversation about corporate greed have to go hand-inhand,” she says. ​ “ Because truly that is who is pricing us out of our homes.” In a July 2024 speech before the NAACP’s annual convention, then President Joe Biden struck an unexpectedly populist note on housing. Speaking in Las Vegas, where rents had increased more than twice as fast as wages over the preceding four-year period, Biden pitched a new plan to withhold federal tax write-offs from large landlords that raise rents by more than 5 % annually — a form of national rent stabilization, more or less, that drew cheers from progressives and backlash from the real estate industry. The last-ditch July 2024 rent cap announcement was part of a bid to shore up support from progressive standard-bearers for Biden’s re-election campaign as questions about his mental fitness mounted. (Squinting at the teleprompter in Las Vegas, Biden actually garbled the plan’s details and told the crowd that corporate landlords wouldn’t be able to raise rents by more than $ 55 a month.) Tenant organizers saw a presidential candidate talking about rent caps as a welcome rhetorical opening. But the actual policy intervention was ​ “ too little and way too late” to register with voters, says Tara Raghuveer, director of the Tenant Union Federation, a national organization that spent the waning months of the Biden administration pushing for stronger federal action to protect tenants, including by attaching rent caps to federally backed apartment loans. Former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris speaks at a North Carolina rally in August 2024, soon after accepting the party’s nomination. PHOTO BY JACEK BOCZARSKI/ANADOLU VIA GETTY IMAGES In the early years of the pandemic, the Biden administration allocated an unprecedented $ 46 . 6 billion in emergency rental assistance, making more than 12 million payments to households at risk of eviction. But this lifeline was blunted by broader dynamics in the rental market, as corporate landlords routinely flouted state and federal eviction moratoria while helping drive double-digit rent increases through alleged price-fixing using the real estate software RealPage, now the subject of multiple antitrust lawsuits. In 2022 , the share of renters considered cost-burdened rose to nearly 50 %, with a record high of 22 . 4 million households spending more than 30 % of their income on rent. Inaction on landlord profiteering exemplifies the grave political miscalculation that helped pave the way for President Donald Trump’s return to the White House, according to Raghuveer. While the Biden administration focused on selling voters on the idea that ​ “ Bidenomics is working, the stock market is great, jobs numbers are up,” that upbeat message ignored ​ “ the real pain that everyday people were feeling every month when they paid their rent,” she says. Soon after the July 2024 rent cap announcement, of course, Biden would drop out and be replaced by then Vice President Kamala Harris as the party’s new de facto nominee. At her first major campaign rally in Atlanta, Harris delivered a fiery speech pledging to take on corporate landlords and ​ “ cap unfair rent increases,” stoking speculation that she would stay the course charted by Biden’s eleventh-hour populism. But after her nomination became official, Harris pivoted toward middle-of-the-road economic messaging and embarked on an ill-fated quest to reach Republican voters through conservative campaign surrogates like former U.S. Rep. Liz Cheney​.An ad in which Harris looked straight at the camera while pledging to ​ “ crack down on landlords who are charging too much” performed best at persuading voters, according to message testing by the firm Blue Rose Research, but rarely aired. Harris did release and campaign on a plan to lower housing costs by building 3 million units nationwide. The plan focused primarily on supply-side solutions like tax incentives for homebuilding and an expansion of the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), which has subsidized millions of apartments classified as ​ “ affordable” nationwide. But there’s an open secret about the nation’s go-to affordable housing program: It’s rarely actually affordable. Because allowable rents are pegged to area median incomes, not tenants’ actual incomes, more than 40 % of LIHTC residents are cost-burdened, according to program data. From the program’s early days, analysts warned that tax credits were a fundamentally inefficient way to subsidize housing. A 1992 analysis by the Congressional Budget Office concluded that the program was ​ “ more suited to the needs of investors than poor renters.” Supply-side housing solutions are also a difficult sell politically. ​ “ Telling people about hundreds of thousands of units that are going to be built years from now, that’s not good politics,” Raghuveer says. ​ “ That doesn’t resonate with people who can’t pay their rent today.” That doesn’t mean that those urging stronger renter protections shun supply-side measures. A burgeoning social housing movement seeks to resolve what its proponents see as a key contradiction in the debate over housing supply: Rents are set, in part, to satisfy the returns expected by for-profit housing financiers, so when rent growth begins to slow, financing for new housing may start to dry up. Expanding options for public financing, development and ownership of housing could help fulfill the promise of building our way to greater affordability. Alongside boosting supply, tenant organizers — and a growing number of economists — are continuing to make the case that the federal government must play a role in protecting tenants from landlord price gouging. Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) speaks during an April 29 news conference rolling out the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ affordability agenda. PHOTO BY PETER ZAY/ANADOLU VIA GETTY IMAGES In 2023 , more than 30 economists signed a letter to the Federal Housing Finance Agency, backing tenant organizers’ call to attach rent caps to federal financing. ​ “ At its core, rent regulations are aimed at rebalancing the power dynamics between tenants and landlords, which disproportionately favor landlords,” the letter read. Neoclassical economists have been nearly unanimous in their rejection of rent control. But the signatories also argued that the debate over rent regulation is reaching the same inflection point as the one surrounding the minimum wage in the 1990 s, when a series of empirical studies concluded that wage hikes were not leading to job losses, as both mainstream economists and business lobbies had predicted they would. In July, Mark Paul, an associate professor at Rutgers University and one of the letter’s signatories, proposed a framework for national rent control that would limit annual increases to 3 % or three-quarters of the local Consumer Price Index, whichever is lower — and apply those limits to all rental housing nationwide, including single-family homes and manufactured housing. Paul also proposed establishing regional boards to enforce the policy and assess whether additional increases are needed to maintain housing quality. The standard economic objection to capping rents is that it distorts markets, ultimately harming renters by discouraging new construction. Anisha Steephen, a former Biden Treasury Department adviser and current fellow at the Roosevelt Institute, contends that something closer to the inverse is true: Housing markets are already distorted by the kind of rampant speculation that helped drive runaway rent increases during the pandemic. Rent regulation doesn’t just protect tenants; it can also act as a form of financial regulation important for broader economic stability. That’s because rents aren’t set according to what prospective tenants can afford; they’re determined by the cash flow landlords need to pay off their often-risky mortgage loans. Similar to ability-to-repay rules for home mortgage lending enacted in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, ​ “ rent regulation exposes where lending has overpromised on the ability of landlords to increase rents in perpetuity,” Steephen says. Absent financial regulation, Steephen says the apartment market could be at risk of the same kind of calamity that occurred in owner-occupied housing after 2008 . Take the 2023 collapse of Signature Bank, the fourth-largest bank failure in U.S. history. The bank had become an aggressive lender for some of New York City’s most notorious landlords, with many of the loans ​ “ predicated on plans for displacing rent-regulated tenants,” according to then New York City Comptroller Brad Lander, who reviewed the bank’s portfolio after it collapsed and the city intervened. Beyond staving off disaster, rent regulation can also open up opportunities for ownership by the public sector, cooperatives or nonprofits otherwise unable to compete in an environment of aggressive speculation. When you have a limit on speculation, Steephen says, ​ “ you allow a broader universe of actors that may meet more mission-aligned goals to participate in the housing market.” In early August, a billboard unveiled in New York City’s Times Square pronounced Mayor Zohran Mamdani the ​ “ Florida Economic Developer of the Year.” The ad winked at a favorite narrative of the business interests that paid for it: that Mamdani’s economic agenda — first and foremost, a recently approved two-year rent freeze — would send taxpayers running toward the more predictable politics of the Sunshine State. But just a week later, supporters waving ​ “ Freeze the Rent” signs broke into cheers as Angie Nixon, a member of Florida’s House of Representatives, notched a stunning victory in the state’s primary to become its Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate. Outspent 13 to one — a jaw-dropping margin even in a record-shatteringly expensive election cycle — Nixon ran a campaign laser-focused on affordability, calling for a national rent freeze, Medicare for All and universal childcare. That message found fertile ground in the state’s lowest-income and least college-educated counties, according to a Washington Post analysis, defying the trends that have often beleaguered progressive candidates. Nixon’s full-throated endorsements of national rent stabilization may have been an especially easy sell in a state whose renters are the most cost-burdened in the nation, thanks to a combination of rising rents and flat wages. She ​ “ speaks about affordability in a real way, the way that our members have been asking about for such a long time,” says Cynthia Laurent, a housing justice campaigner with the nonprofit Florida Rising. Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon campaigns in Miami on August 29. Nixon’s platform includes a call to freeze rents nationwide. PHOTO BY JOE RAEDLE/GETTY IMAGES In 2022 , the group was part of a coalition that attempted to enact emergency rent stabilization in Orange County, Fla., where rents were rising sharply despite ample housing supply. Voters approved the measure overwhelmingly, but it never took effect thanks to a lawsuit brought by landlords. The following year, Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a law preempting local passage of rent stabilization and most other tenant protections. Florida Rising’s 501 (c)( 4 ) arm has endorsed Nixon. Nixon is now among a handful of congressional candidates testing the strength of their affordability message against Republican opponents in November, after making federal rent caps and tenant protections key tenets of their primary campaigns. In Tennessee, after Republicans redrew electoral maps to carve up the state’s last blue district covering Memphis, State Rep. Justin Pearson is pitching the white, rural voters he must now appeal to on his vision for affordability — including a data center moratorium, federal minimum wage increase, rent caps and massive federal investment in affordable housing. And in Michigan, tenant organizer Will Lawrence is running in a district where Trump won by just one point in 2024 , making it a top pickup prospect for Democrats. A co-founder of the youth climate group Sunrise Movement, Lawrence also spent the last several years helping to build tenant unions and win new renter protections through the statewide coalition Michigan Rent Is Too Damn High. Under the state’s Democratic trifecta from 2023 to 2024 , the coalition hoped to pass a suite of new housing affordability measures, including removal of the state’s ban on rent control and a $ 4 billion allocation for social housing as part of a state push to build tens of thousands of new homes. While the coalition did win some new tenant protections and funding for affordable housing, Lawrence says it was a ​ “ drop in the bucket” compared to the scope of the crisis. If elected to Congress, Lawrence says he would push for a federal tenant bill of rights and ​ “ a new generation of public housing for the 21 st century,” modeled after the success of publicly financed, mixed-income developments in Montgomery County, Md. Lawrence’s approach to running on affordability is to get specific. ​ “ No voter says, ​ ‘ I have an affordability problem,’” he notes. ​ “ They say, ​ ‘ the rent is too damn high.’ Or ​ ‘ this energy bill is outlandish.’ Or ​ ‘ I just paid $ 17 for three chicken breasts at the grocery store.’” That framing echoes the takeaways of an August poll that found that while 70 % of 2026 Democratic candidates are deploying some form of populist rhetoric, certain messages work better than others. In a survey of more than 6 , 000 adults, conducted by the Center for Working-Class Politics and the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative, kitchen-table populist messages that led with concrete costs, not abstractions about a fair economy, were far more persuasive. By front-loading housing and defining the terrain of affordability, campaigns like Pearson’s and Lawrence’s are helping to create a new political common sense, says the Tenant Union Federation’s Raghuveer: ​ “ You have to talk about housing, you have to talk about tenants, and maybe more specifically than anything, you have to talk about the rent.” “ This is a pain point for everyday Americans in every community in this country, and that’s every congressional district, whether urban, suburban or rural,” she continues. ​ “ It’s a winning issue.”
