articles.title: A Sweeping Reelection Victory for Shawn Fain and His Slate at UAW
articles.content: United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain is poised to win a second four-year term, with an overwhelming lead in member balloting for the union’s top officers. The election was a referendum on the new fighting direction Fain has taken the union by leading 2023 ’s Stand-Up Strike against the Big 3 automakers, other bold contract fights and new organizing campaigns. It marks the second time members have voted for their top officers in the union’s 91 years. UAW members voted to switch to a one-member-one-vote system in December 2021 . Fain took more than two-thirds of the vote, against five opponents. His nearest competitor, incumbent vice president Rich Boyer, had around 13 %. Fain is running as part of the United UAW slate. His slate-mate for secretary-treasurer, Brandon Campbell, has also garnered two-thirds, against two rivals including incumbent Margaret Mock. The slate’s candidates for the three vice president spots appeared on track to be elected with 19 - 25 % each in a field of 11 candidates. (VP candidates need 16 . 7 % to win.) The slate has also won all the regional director races counted thus far that it contested. If the slate sweeps, as appears likely, it will hold all the seats on the union’s International Executive Board except for one regional director. Fain has won a majority of the vote in most locals, from assembly plants to legal services, and a plurality in almost all the rest. Boyer, who heads the union’s Stellantis division, has won just two of the union’s dozens of big locals: Local 140 , Warren Truck, his home local, and Local 1700 at Sterling Heights Assembly Plant, both near Detroit. Turnout was low and similar to the 2022 election, with roughly 10 % of the union’s 400 , 000 active members and 600 , 000 retirees returning their mail ballots. (Retirees also vote on top officers in the UAW.) While some expected Fain’s strongest support to come from the higher education and legal aid locals on the East Coast, turnout there was down by more than half from 2022 , with fewer than 2 , 000 ballots counted. Turnout was up in Local 4811 at the University of California, which went 75 % for Fain, but still only 2 , 500 of 60 , 000 members there voted. As in the last election, it was members in the big manufacturing locals that were key to Fain’s victory. Perennially online candidate Brian Keller had 7 % of the presidential vote. As the ballots were counted he took to Facebook Live to swear at members for 30 minutes and call them ​ “ morons” for not voting for him. Motivators In phone interviews with a dozen members, auto workers cited pensions and post-retirement health care as their key motivators for backing Fain. They also raised concerns about tackling automation and job security. But the biggest issue was the better contracts the UAW has won since Fain took office. Infighting between Fain and his opponents on the outgoing International Executive Board — Rich Boyer, Margaret Mock and Mike Booth — came up, but people drew widely different conclusions, with many repeating the phrase Fain ​ “ isn’t perfect.” Jeep worker Megan Fagan in Toledo said some members have checked out due to the internal drama, reinforcing the cynical view that not much has changed. For most, though, disagreements at headquarters were not of interest or on their radar. They looked at their pay stubs and voted accordingly. Boyer, Mock, and Booth came together to form the Integrity Slate but failed to offer a counter to Fain’s focus on fighting the companies and launching new organizing drives. Boyer’s main pitches in his campaign statement in the UAW magazine were to lower union dues and reduce the staff at union headquarters. “ Fain and his slate are the only ones that have a real program for the future of the union,” said historian Nelson Lichtenstein, author of Walter Reuther: The Most Dangerous Man in Detroit . ​ “ You’d think the other people would have come up with something aside from they want to reduce dues, which means basically cripple the new organizing.” “ The members chose Fain, despite the Monitor’s best efforts to create turbulence, because we’re ready to fight for retirement health care and protection from A.I. layoffs in 2028 ,” said Gary Chynoweth, vice chair of the reform network UAW Member Action , in a statement. ​ “ Our work now is to keep helping members step up as leaders in a union that’s ready to fight.” Keep on track UAW Local 551 member Candyla Brown is one of 5 , 000 workers at Ford’s assembly plant in Chicago. She said she backed the United UAW slate to keep the union on track in 2028 , to win pensions, post-retirement health care, and pay bumps that keep up with inflation. To win these demands, ​ “ we need strong leadership,” she said. ​ “ We had a good experience with the 2023 strike, and I’ve been watching the new organizing efforts,” she said. ​ “ I think the UAW has come a long way since Fain got into office.” She pointed to her own local’s successful organizing of nurses at her plant and a narrowly lost election at Julian Electric, a parts plant that supplies Ford, as examples of how the union is devoting resources to organize, even if some campaigns have come up short. She said organizing in the South is another bright spot. Volkswagen workers in Tennessee voted to join the UAW in 2024 and won a first contract earlier this year, becoming the first unionized foreign-owned auto assembly plant in the South. Jessica Acosta of Ford Local 249 outside of Kansas City said she voted for Fain and his slate because she’s seen transparency at the top of the union and wants to see the same in her local, where there was a contested election recently. ​ “ I want to know what’s going on,” she said. ​ “ I don’t want to be left in the dark.” Her top priority is winning pensions, though she recognizes that’s a tough demand to win. At Daimler Truck in North Carolina, Jon Greene, president of Local 3520 , said workers are building about 80 trucks a day, after winning a new record contract in 2024 with 25 percent wage bumps and job security. Their contract expires in March 2028 . In the next one, Local 3520 wants to win more product for the plant to ensure job security, especially after Daimler shut down a Freightliner truck plant in Oregon. But the company is slated to open another plant on the East Coast in 2029 . ​ “ So it’s important that we put the right people in place, or keep them in place, who know what they’re doing to get us to 2028 ,” he said. He said Daimler has staffed up its labor relations personnel in preparation for another showdown, and corporate HR has been closely following the election. ​ “ We tripped them up with the last contract,” said Greene. ​ “ It wasn’t any more of that friendly bargaining that had been happening over the years with International, so we caught them off guard.” Temp workers converted Kirk Hoddinott started as a temp line worker in 2020 at Toledo Jeep in Ohio, building Jeep Wranglers and Gladiators. Toledo Jeep was one of the plants that launched the Stand-Up Strike, which forced Stellantis to convert all temporary workers to permanent roles after nine months on the job. Hoddinott became one of 1 , 957 temps at Stellantis who were converted within three months of ratification. In spite of the 2023 contract’s big gains, he said, the lingering effects of past corruption scandals contribute to cynicism among Local 12 members who blame reps for poor communication in grievance handling. ​ “ People still think that the union is in bed with the company because they feel that they’re not being represented as strongly as they want to be,” said Hoddinott. “ I would like to see more communication through our union from top to bottom, and back from bottom to top,” he said, ​ “ because I think that the company is talking to each other, and they’re making a game plan. I think we should be doing the same thing.” Nonetheless, Hoddinott said he believes Fain has made ​ “ good progress” and ​ “ I want to see another term and see how much more progress that he can really make.” Hoddinott’s top priorities are post-retirement health insurance and job security around automation. ​ “ Every person that works there for more than 10 years is going to have wear and tear in their body that you’re going to have permanent health problems from,” he said. Before the massive concessions of 2007 , Big 3 retirees had company-paid health insurance until they were eligible for Medicare. Those hired since then no longer do. He worries when he reads news stories about humanoid robots at BMW plants. At the Jeep complex, ​ “ they have a robot that can go up and down the racks and look at inventory to try to find parts,” he said, ​ “ and they are telling me that so far it hasn’t taken any jobs.” Renewed mandate With a renewed mandate, the pressure is on Fain’s team to organize members to step up when contracts expire at the Big 3 automakers on May 1 , 2028 . In 2023 , the companies were caught off guard, accustomed to a sedate strike, if any, and modest union demands. When the union launched a spreading strike against all three companies at once, with more plants walking out week by week, company bargainers were blindsided. They gave up more in that one contract than they had in the previous four contracts combined. They will likely be better prepared for May Day 2028 . Unions may face another obstacle in 2028 — in an election year, Democratic politicians traditionally bring heavy pressure not to rock the boat, fearing blame from voters. In 2023 , though, a poll found 75 % of Americans supported the UAW’s strike. Some expensive union demands were left on the table last time: pensions and retiree health insurance for workers hired after the big concessions of 2007 - 2009 , and protections against mandatory overtime and automation. Flush with victory in fall 2023 , Fain urged other unions to line up their contracts with the Big 3 ’s, for a united assault on corporate coffers. Dominick Moss, a member of Local 1853 at General Motors’ Spring Hill, Tennessee, assembly plant, said he backed United UAW because it built a broad coalition and set a goal of preparing for a potential May Day 2028 general strike. “ I think that we have a solid ground laid in terms of how we’ve been connecting with other unions,” Moss said. ​ “ If enough of us go on strike, we could get more attention on universal health care. I would like to see Medicare for All and the PRO Act passed. I would like to see consequences for corporations doing rampant automation.” (The PRO Act would make it easier for workers to organize and secure contracts.) Moss said his plant’s chassis department in general assembly lost 38 jobs as a direct result of automation over the last couple of years. ​ “ Cameras replaced quality gates,” he said. ​ “ All of the seat loading is done by robots now, and my team was previously loading seats.” The Spring Hill assembly plant builds electric vehicles like the Cadillac Lyriq, and they aren’t selling as well after Trump and congressional Republicans eliminated a $ 7 , 500 tax credit. ​ “ When the price of those electric cars went up about $ 8 , 000 overnight, we started selling less of them,” he said. Ditching the tax credit also had an impact at the Chattanooga Volkswagen plant, where Zach Costello, who backed Fain, said ​ “ there have been massive cutbacks.” Volkswagen stopped producing the company’s ID. 4 SUV in April, instead ramping up production of the gas-powered Atlas SUV. Government hands off UAW The election results are a sharp rebuke to the government-appointed monitor , Neil Barofsky, whose original mandate was to oversee clean-up of the endemic corruption that sent 13 union officials to jail. Barofsky developed a strong antagonism to Fain when the UAW Executive Board passed a resolution calling for a ceasefire in Gaza in late 2023 , which the monitor said could be seen as ​ “ antisemitic.” Fain resisted Barofsky’s attempts to reverse that stance. Ever since, Barofsky has issued a series of reports criticizing Fain and siding with his opponents on the Board. Some UAW members who followed the drama drew cynical conclusions, but apparently most voters found Fain’s actions spoke louder than the monitor’s words. Barofsky’s mandate is set to end in early 2027 , but the consent decree keeps open the possibility of extending the monitorship. If Barofsky’s previous behavior is any indication, he may push to stay in place longer. Fain’s opponents made much of the monitor’s reports, which accused Fain of misdeeds including retaliating against Boyer and Mock, after he relieved them of some of their major responsibilities. Opponents spent most of their energy attacking him personally and detailing their own grievances, rather than talking about the direction of the union. Their campaigns did not have much reach. Fain, on the other hand, reminded members of the union’s achievements and tried to keep the disagreements from looking personal. Despite encouraging leadership at the top, the UAW has a long way to go to become a member-driven union that consistently takes on the boss. While Fain has charted a new direction, much of the union bears the scars of decades of concessions, or is still stuck in the old, company-friendly ways of operating. That includes seeing the union structure as a career ladder, a way to get off the factory floor. Years of one-party rule means that the bench of members able and willing to push the union in a new direction is still shallow. That has the potential to change in locals where the International has brought big resources for contract campaigns and strikes. The UAW Member Action network is slowly working, through education and trainings, to build up the bench. After this election, it looks like the UAW will continue to be back in the fight. articles.title: “They’re Trying to Starve Us”: BP Opposes Unemployment Benefits for Locked-Out Workers
articles.content: WHITING, IND.— Six and a half months after being locked out of his job as a British Petroleum (BP) operator, Jon is still showing up to picket shifts. I met him on the side of a road, the refinery spewing smoke behind him. For a while, unemployment benefits of around $ 335 a week helped ease the financial burden, he tells me, but those went away at the end of September when he hit the six-month mark. And now, BP is appealing the locked-out workers’ unemployment with the state of Indiana. It’s a move that could result in workers like Jon having to pay back the assistance they’ve already received. The appeal comes on top of a bruising lockout that has left some families dependent on donated pantry items for food, diapers and toilet paper. “ British Petroleum made a deliberate choice to challenge our members’ unemployment benefits after the Indiana Department of Workforce Development determined they were eligible, says Eric Schultz, president of USW Local 7 - 1 , which represents the locked-out workers. ​ “ It is another attempt to increase financial pressure on our members and their families and achieve through economic coercion what the company has been unable to achieve at the bargaining table.” For Jon, who asked to use only his first name to protect his privacy, the impact can be measured in time: ​ “ My wife asked me, ​ ‘ What do you think this is going to cost us?’” he says, standing next to an industrial drum with a small fire burning inside. A sign reading ​ “ illegal lockout” leans against a nearby folding chair. ​ “ I said it’s going to cost us two years. And she said, ​ ‘ Well, you think you’re going to be out two years?’ I said, ​ ‘ No, but no matter how long we’re out, we’re not putting money in any 401 (k)s. We’re not doing this. We’re not doing that. I wanted to retire at 60 years old — now, I know I probably at least got to work ​ ’ till 62 , or maybe longer.’” BP’s unemployment appeal is one more piece of evidence that the company is trying to starve out its workforce, rather than engage in good-faith bargaining, workers told me during an October 6 visit to the union hall and picket lines. USW 7 - 1 members say they are in an existential battle for their union, against a company that wants to constrict their ability to strike, expand management’s power to unilaterally set conditions and tear the local away from pattern bargaining, USW’s joint bargaining with the oil and gas industry. Since around 800 workers were kicked out on March 19 , the union says, replacement workers have been laboring inside the facility, while locked-out workers maintain a 24 / 7 picket outside. The union is determined to continue fighting back, even as the company, whose quarterly profit doubled to over $ 5 billion the previous quarter, intensifies its economic pressure. “ They want to have it both ways,” Jon says of his job. He’s missed birthdays, weddings, holidays and even slept in the parking lot after an 18 -hour shift to avoid missing the next one, he tells me. The job can be treacherous; it’s a workplace where there’s a risk of fires and even explosions, he says. ​ “ How can you ask everything out of us and then show us such little respect in return?” When I first met locked-out BP operator Michelle O’Shaughnessy in July, she had been at the union hall since 4 a.m., signing people in for picket duty and helping run the pantry. When I walked in on October 6 , I found her sitting in the same spot. This time she had been picketing all night, then at the union hall all morning. Her next shift will run from midnight to 3 p.m.” None of the locked-out workers get paid for their time picketing or supporting the fightback. But in addition to the pantry, there is a hardship fund locked-out workers can apply to for help paying for specific bills, with funds supplied by the USW International and local unions. Still, families are hurting. O’Shaughnessy coordinates food, transportation, and the hall’s schedule, so she has a strong sense of workers’ needs. Supplies in the pantry have been going fast, she says. ​ “ We did get in some toilet paper, and it’s gone within a couple shifts of people coming in and out because it’s a basic need. Cleaning products, personal care products, besides the food products, are all things that you still need as a family.” “ We’ve had a lot of babies since we’ve been out, and a lot of them actually have under-two-year-olds on top of it, so you got two children in diapers at the same time.” In Indiana, unemployment benefits last for up to 26 weeks, and workers are now bumping up against this limit. ​ “ The people that started filing right away, they’re running out of their allocated number of weeks,” says Schultz, as we sit in his office at the union hall. ​ “ There’s others that didn’t file right away, so it’ll be a slow drop-off.” Outside the BP refinery plant in Whiting, Ind. Photo by Sarah Lazare According to Schultz, ​ “ the Indiana Department of Workforce Development had to make an initial decision on whether or not our members qualified for unemployment insurance due to the lockout, which in Indiana is a very gray area.” The union ​ “ had a team of lawyers from Pittsburgh and Indianapolis working initially to try to ensure that we did qualify for the unemployment, and we were granted it,” he explains. ​ “ The Department of Workforce Development made their initial ruling saying that yeah, you’re entitled to it.” But now, the company is appealing. On October 2 , the union released a statement saying, ​ “ If the company’s appeal is granted, United Steelworkers Local 7 - 1 members will lose the roughly $ 310 a week in unemployment benefits they are now taking home. Worse, they could be required to pay back unemployment benefits they’ve already received.” The union is calling on Gov. Mike Braun, ​ “ who oversees the agency that decides unemployment appeals, to reject the company’s effort,” the union’s statement says. State Sen. Rodney Pol Jr. (D-Ind.) and Rep. Chuck Moseley (D-Ind.), meanwhile, are proposing legislation to protect the unemployment benefits of locked-out workers like those at BP. “ Unemployment is $ 390 a week, and that’s before taxes,” Schultz says. ​ “ So depending on how much you have coming out on taxes, it’s around $ 310 to $ 335 per week, which is not a lot. But it means a lot for those that are receiving it. From a company standpoint, it’s drops in the bucket. It’s unconscionable that they would even appeal it. Why not just let it go and continue with your lockout if you insist, which we don’t agree with, obviously? They didn’t need to do this.” “ It’s salt in the wounds,” he says. When asked to comment on the appeal, a BP spokesperson said the company ​ “ does not comment on ongoing legal matters,” though they did say ​ “ it’s not unusual to challenge unemployment benefit awards, as BP did here. Any decision ultimately sits with the state.” The spokesperson added that ​ “ BP has continued to provide certain benefits to our employees throughout the current lockout, including medical, dental and vision coverage.” But Jon said of the company, ​ “ Appealing unemployment benefits after they’re pretty much done? There’s nothing that leads me to believe that anything they’ve done is out of benevolence or care or concern for the workforce.” In the meantime, families’ stress is increasing as the holidays approach. ​ “ You have first Christmases, you have second Christmases, and things like that,” O’Shaughnessy says. Some members of the community are talking about setting up angel trees to make sure workers struggling to afford holiday gifts for their families get donations, she says. After a handful of bargaining sessions in September and early October, there have been ​ “ some new faces at the table,” but nothing has fundamentally changed, says Schultz. ​ “ They’re not offering proposals. They’re offering a ransom letter to say this is what it’s going to take to get your jobs back.” Throughout negotiations, the union has been concerned about management’s support for an industrial ​ “ peace” clause that would require 150 days’ notice for a strike. This measure would dramatically undermine the union’s ability to use this tool to protect conditions. And proposals to protect ​ “ management rights” to unilaterally determine workers’ conditions ​ “ are huge,” Schultz says. ​ “ They’re just trying to completely isolate us and strip away what it means to be a union: bargaining rights, seniority protections, layoff protections, job bidding language. They want to be able to select who gets the highest-paying jobs instead of going by a bidding process that includes seniority.” The company posted a video update on October 6 in which Chris DellaFranco, the Whiting refinery manager, said BP made proposals that ​ “ would allow us to better partner with companies that specialize in tools that can unlock improvements that we never thought were possible before. I’m talking about using technology to advance safety, efficiency, production and reliability — important goals for our refinery.” But Schultz said, ​ “ I don’t even know what that means. It just seems like it’s just more corporate spin, and just them throwing out euphemisms to try to justify eliminating jobs and eliminate our bargaining rights.” According to an October 1 email update to members from the USW Local 7 - 1 Board of Directors, ​ “ the company has made no meaningful movement on the core proposals,” which caused 98 . 3 % of the membership to reject management’s ​ “ last, best and final” offer on March 2 . (Members rejected a revised settlement, too, and when the union gave a counteroffer on March 17 , the company responded with a lockout, according to USW.) ​ “ More than six months later, we are still spending bargaining sessions discussing the same proposals,” the update read. A BP spokesperson told me the company ​ “ is committed to ongoing negotiations to reach a ratified agreement that will bring our USW 7 - 1 represented employees back to work and support Whiting’s long-term future. The way for that to happen is for USW 7 - 1 ’s elected representatives to meet us at the bargaining table and give members the opportunity to vote on a proposal.” But Schultz says, ​ “ Meeting at the bargaining table just to agree to the company’s concessionary demands isn’t bargaining.” He adds, ​ “ The company’s subsequent proposals have only been worse. The company needs to listen to their employees, the public and community leaders and get serious about bargaining — in good faith. Not demanding surrender with a proverbial gun to our heads.” Brian Davis, a BP operations specialist, was feeling sick but still showed up to his shift as a driver of a bus that transports locked-out workers to picket lines scattered around the refinery. Just that day, he found out he lost his unemployment while filling out his voucher. ​ “ I thought I still had one more week, but apparently not,” he tells me. He rides a motorcycle to ​ “ de-stress.” Losing unemployment, he says, means ​ “ not being able to be here to help out all my brothers and sisters. It kind of sucks.” Being at the hall makes him ​ “ informed about what’s going on,” he explains. ​ “ Are they meeting? Not meeting? If they are, what’s going on with the talks? They give out email updates every so often, but being here every day, you hear some of the rumors and stuff like that. Some good, some not so good.” “ They’re trying to starve us out to make us desperate and succumb to their demands.” The union says the lockout is illegal and has filed 15 unfair labor practice charges with the National Labor Relations Board, accusing the company of acts that include surveillance, coercive statements and refusal to bargain in good faith. But in the meantime, they are still prevented from working. ​ “ Everyone’s dealing with stress and anxiety and fear and questions of the unknown and the issues that it creates at home, the issues that it creates internally with people, mental health, things like that. We’re certainly feeling the effects of it, but it hasn’t made its waiver at all,” Schultz says. It’s been easier for maintenance employees to find jobs, says Schultz, ​ “ because a lot of them had still maintained their journeyman’s cards through a building trade.” But operations, he says, ​ “ is a little bit trickier because it’s just such a niche job.” Some workers have moved on, while a core of workers keeps the pickets going. A bulletin board in the union hall is covered with letters of solidarity from around the country, including one impassioned handwritten note from a Cornell graduate student who is a member of United Electrical Workers Local 300 . Schultz says one local in Delaware writes his union a monthly $ 20 , 000 check. Davis tells me it’s a ​ “ bad day” of picketing, but the hall fills with people during the mid-day shift change. Some watch a movie projected on a screen, while others joke and chat. The hall has an air of familiarity and ease; these are people who have spent a lot of time with each other and have an established routine. In mid-August, this community was one of several across Northwest Indiana hit by severe storms that shut off power in the area for around 12 days, workers told me. ​ “ We had no power at the hall, people didn’t have power at home, so we just shifted to just trying to help the community, and we shut down our picketing for two weeks,” Schultz told me. ( Studies show that storms like these will grow more frequent and severe amid worsening climate change, which is itself driven by fossil fuel companies like BP.) Other than that, the union is out on the lines, save major holidays. Maintaining pickets is a way that workers can signal to the company that it will not fold to economic pressure: that it is a powerful force that must be bargained with, and united in demands for good-faith negotiations. But sticking with the fight is not easy. When I ask Jon what it’s been like to lose unemployment, he says, ​ “ Pick a bill. … Everything’s getting more expensive.” Even still, he says he plans to keep coming out to picket, and he also sometimes drives the picket van. It helps that his wife, a nurse, is bringing in money for the family. The stakes are high. Workers worry that BP is testing the power of companies to completely crush their workforce’s union. Akshay Patel, an inspector, stands next to Jon on the line. ​ “ In my 15 years, I always thought that this is the job where I can retire. This is my dream job. This is the place where my family and my kids and everybody looked to. This lockout was a wake-up call, as well as a shock wave across my whole entire family. I never expected this company to do that to me and my family.” Patel’s wife works a minimum wage job, and due to hardship from the lockout, he has taken out loans to cover his daughter’s tuition for college. ​ “ They want to bring us to our knees in one way or another, because as an individual you don’t have billions of dollars backing like this big corporation.” “ We will not give up,” he says. ​ “ We will keep fighting until we get our bargaining rights.” This article is a joint publication of In These Times and Workday Magazine , a nonprofit newsroom devoted to holding the powerful accountable through the perspective of workers.

articles.title: From the Green Line to the Yellow Line: A Story of Colonization in Palestine
articles.content: In October 2025 , a ceasefire agreement between Israel and the Palestinian factions was supposed to bring calm to a Gaza devastated by genocide. Instead, Israel has continued to violate the ceasefire, murdering more than a thousand Palestinians since the agreement began and usurping more land via the ​ “ yellow line” — an arbitrary line splitting the Gaza Strip into eastern and western halves. A year since the ceasefire, Israel has continued to push the yellow line inwards and now controls nearly 70 percent of the Gaza Strip and continues to kill Palestinians on a daily basis simply for being near the arbitrary line. Ahmad, a father of two who lives near the yellow line in Al-Tuffah in Gaza City, talked about how difficult life is for Palestinians living near the yellow line. “ It’s a very painful feeling to be living in your own home, with only moments separating you from death,” he said. ​ “ We’re constantly hit by gunfire, missile shrapnel, and explosions. It’s a very difficult feeling when you’re in your home and never feel safe for even a minute.” According to the ceasefire agreement, the yellow line was intended to only demarcate the first stage of Israeli troop withdrawal, but it’s become the de facto border of Gaza and now Israel has constructed gates, sandy embankments and military posts along the yellow line suggesting preparations for a more permanent militarized frontier. For Palestinians, the yellow line is only the most recent chapter in colonial violence. Growing up in Gaza, the ​ “ green line” circumscribed our lives and separated Palestinians from one another and from the world. In 1949 , Israel agreed on new borders for Palestine with Egypt, Jordan, Syria, and Lebanon. These borders, like the state of Israel itself, were created just a year prior on the ruins of 530 Palestinian towns and villages. The line, drawn with the help of U.S. diplomat and mediator Ralph Bunche , defined Israel’s new borders and became known as the green line for one simple reason: Bunche used a green marker to draw it. The green line also marked the boundary of the West Bank. Following Israel’s occupation of the Gaza Strip and the West Bank in 1967 , the entire territory came under Israeli control. As time passed, Israel pushed and blurred the boundaries of the green line with bypass roads and settlements built on top of and displacing Palestinian towns and communities. Over the years, Israel’s green line swallowed approximately 200 square kilometers of Gaza, more than a third of Gaza’s territory under the 1949 agreement. In reality, the green line had no color. My mother once traveled from Gaza to the West Bank, and my uncle asked her to meet him at the green line on the West Bank side. She kept searching the area for something green but found nothing. After wandering around for nearly an hour, she finally found my uncle and learned that the green line did not actually have a color at all. The ​ “ line” was simply a fiction created by Israeli colonizers, made real by brutal violence and internalized by colonized people as an act of survival. A green line drawn in marker on a map has profoundly shaped the lives of Palestinians. In 2018 , hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza marched every week to that arbitrary line demarcating the Israeli border, calling on the world to end Israel’s blockade of Gaza and recognize their rights as refugees in mass marches called the Great March of Return. These nonviolent protests were organized and attended by a cross section of Palestinian civil society. Israel responded with lethal force, killing more than 200 marchers and injuring more than 20 , 000 for getting near that line. For the last three years, Palestinians in Gaza have been subjected to a new and terrifying onslaught of lines, zones, and borders that became a core feature in Israel’s genocide. Israel divided the Gaza Strip into blocs, assigning each area a number to make it easier for the Israeli military to issue evacuation orders. Israel dropped millions of leaflets on Gaza marking blocs for immediate evacuation and demolitions, sending waves of displacement and fear among Palestinians. The blocs were marked with red; Palestinians were given only a few hours to leave. At the same time, Israel split Gaza into two main sections, the north and the south, ordering Palestinians to leave the northern part of the Strip. This division was enforced through a military corridor stretching from the Mediterranean coast in western Gaza to its eastern border, passing through the site of the former Israeli settlement of Netzarim, which existed until Israel’s 2005 disengagement. The corridor consequently became known as the Netzarim Corridor. My colleagues and family members in Gaza were forcibly displaced dozens of times, traveling dangerous roads with thousands of others with no guarantee their destination would be safer than the neighborhoods being pummeled by airstrikes behind them. In 2025 , the Israeli military deployed yellow concrete blocks to mark the yellow line. These blocks have become a nightmare for people in Gaza because they keep moving. In many cases, Palestinians living near the yellow line have woken up to find that soldiers have moved the blocks further into their neighborhoods, placing their homes inside the newly expanded zone. Overnight, their homes were now in an area under direct Israeli military control. And the moving line has continued to consume more and more of Gaza’s fertile agricultural land, contributing to the starvation of Palestinians. Arwa, an educator from Gaza who lives near the yellow line in Deir Al-Balah, said the constantly moving nature of the line has made it nearly impossible for Palestinians to rebuild the essential aspects of their daily lives. “ We’d be outside trying to enjoy fresh air in the middle of the blazing summer and suddenly we’d hear tanks shooting out of the blue. Shortly, quadcopters would follow and start shooting,” she said, ​ “ Other than the safety of my friends and colleagues, the displacement of so many of our school teachers is making me worried about the school shutting down, one of the last few spaces still providing education for around 600 elementary students and around 800 preparatory students.” The yellow line is Gaza’s newest nightmare. It echoes the violent imposition of the green line in 1949 , yet it’s more expansive, more fluid, and more frightening. Unlike the green line, which marked an armistice boundary, the yellow line continues to move, steadily shrinking the cage that Israel has created for Palestinians in Gaza. Rather than allowing new militarized borders to further confine Palestinians, the world must draw a line against continued violations of international law and the ongoing colonization of Palestinian land. The yellow line should be abolished. It has no place in a just and peaceful future, for Palestinians or for anyone else.

articles.title: Latin America: the ‘cultural battle’ as a facade for neoliberalism
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: For several years now, politicians, influencers, and intellectuals from Latin America’s new radical right have been speaking about the importance of the “cultural battle” to recover a sort of perspective lost in the past and to underpin a civilizational project that prioritizes the individual, individual freedom, and the free market above all else. Probably the first to insist on this idea in the media was Javier Milei, the current president of Argentina, who initially made a name for himself as an economist who had no problem insulting his opponents and defending orthodox neoliberal thought. At that time, Milei, along with his intellectual allies, called for a stand against a purported culture imposed by so-called left-wing elites who had tarnished common sense, Christian morality, and individual freedom, among many other things. A few days ago, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella called for a radicalization of his “cultural battle” and ordered the removal of dozens of works of art from various museums in order to restore a culture that has been held captive by the left, Marxism, and other dark (or, as Milei himself puts it, “demonic”) forces. In reality, the move isn’t particularly original. Back in the United States, Pat Buchanan (a close advisor to Nixon and Reagan) had already advocated for and encouraged inflammatory rhetoric to wage a “culture war” and thus defend a culture tarnished by social change. Among the major intellectual inspirers of this doctrine are the American Sam Francis and the Frenchmen Alain de Benoist and Guillaume Faye (albeit with their well-known differences). Even some Germans in the 1930s attempted to make what they called “cultural Bolshevism” the scapegoat for all their ills. But the push for a “cultural battle” in Latin America had a more interesting rationale. And it is not so much due to a supposed pragmatic interpretation of Antonio Gramsci’s concept of hegemony – which has been distorted by the new radical right, as well as by much of liberalism and social democracy, which understand it solely as “cultural hegemony.” No, in reality, the intention behind invoking a “culture war” against feminism, abortion rights, progressive governments, left-wing artists, revolutionary intellectuals, etc., is more of a strategic nature. For those who are actually, as ideologues, behind the “culture war” projects are not Buchanan, Francis, De Benoist, or Faye, but Hayek, Friedman, and the rest of the neoliberal economists. The truth is that neoliberalism in Latin America during the late 20th and early 21st centuries was both a resounding failure and a magnificent victory. This apparent contradiction is resolved depending on which social class we are discussing. During that time, the most powerful social classes, economically speaking, managed to accumulate an enormous amount of power and resources, the likes of which have rarely been seen in Latin American history. But such a level of accumulation in societies subjugated by a global imperialist order (such as those in Latin America) necessarily drives the working classes into conditions of material precariousness that are almost unbearable. Mass migration, uprisings, deaths, the loss of a lifetime’s savings, rising crime, and so on were just some of the devastation left in the wake of the neoliberalism driven by the Washington Consensus during that period. In response to the crisis, several centrist, center-left, and even leftist leaders won elections in the region in quick succession: Chávez in Venezuela, Morales in Bolivia, Fernández in Argentina, Correa in Ecuador, Lula in Brazil, Bachelet in Chile, Mujica in Uruguay, etc. They sought to resolve a capitalist economic crisis within the framework of capitalism itself, resorting to approaches that combined Keynesian measures with legislation designed to protect and expand rights, especially for the most marginalized sectors. These were times when (not without contradictions with other political forces, including those of a more traditional left) the economies of these countries improved, thanks in part to high commodity prices on the global market. And with public policies that, in many cases, focused on providing aid and social programs, the situation of millions of Latin Americans clearly improved. Between 2000 and 2012 alone, 56 million Latin American citizens managed to rise out of poverty. Once the storm of discontent against neoliberalism had passed, the ruling classes decided they’d had enough of progressive governments. But to regain absolute control (since they had always maintained the necessary share of power to influence national decisions), they needed to win back the governments, and to do so, they found themselves at a crossroads. They knew that the central argument against center-left governments could not be based solely on the economic downturn that followed the end of high prices for Latin American natural resources, but that it had to be grounded in something more – something that would come across as novel, radical, and a sort of conservative revolutionary ideology. And that is how they found in the “culture war” a niche for ideological propaganda that has had a historic impact on Latin America. In addition to the aforementioned criticisms, they succeeded (through their intellectuals, politicians, influencers, media outlets, social media, and so on) in creating a perceived link between progressivism and corruption, between progressivism and organized crime, and, finally, between progressivism and an alleged erosion of individual freedom. But the truth is that these kinds of strategies can cause political upheaval like that seen in the region in recent years, during which (thanks to the support of national and international tycoons, as well as support from Washington and other governments such as Israel’s) there has been a string of victories for the radical right, which could complete its winning hand next Sunday in Brazil. But in the long term, neoliberalism cannot (nor does it intend to) overcome the contradiction inherent in an economy of this nature in countries with clear relationships of international domination. Thus, at the height of this new wave of neoliberal right-wing movements, the first cracks in ideological stability are already beginning to appear, precisely in the face of a material reality that offers no respite from political rhetoric. The situation of millions of Latin Americans (especially the poorest) is rapidly being complicated by a radical increase in the rate of inequality. The promises made by the new right-wing movements to defeat organized crime show no signs of being a reality or of bringing about clear regional change. Perhaps this is what Nietzsche, another great reactionary, meant when he acknowledged that culture is merely the veneer of something deeper. And that veneer is beginning to wear away very slowly – a process that is nonetheless noticeable if one pays attention.

articles.title: Tanzania’s smallholder farmers set their course in Morogoro
articles.author: Jonis Ghedi Alasow
articles.content: Some 850 smallholder farmers from across mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar met in Morogoro from September 29 to October 1 for the National Smallholder Farmers’ Conference and the 31st Annual General Meeting (AGM) of MVIWATA, the network of Tanzania’s smallholder farmers’ groups. The theme was “Towards Food Sovereignty: Land Security, Agroecology and Economic Justice for Smallholder Farmers” (“Kuelekea Uhuru wa Chakula: Uhakika wa Ardhi, Kilimo Ikolojia na Haki Uchumi kwa Wakulima Wadogo”). The AGM is MVIWATA’s highest body. Founded by farmers in 1993, the organization interacted directly with 58,916 farmers last year, 57% of whom were women, according to its own count. Two days of conference debate precede the AGM, allowing members to debate policy before coming together to decide the way forward. For this year’s AGM, MVIWATA farmers took up the key issues of land, markets, seed and, for the first time, carbon trade. Dr Bashiru Ally, Tanzania’s Minister of Livestock and Fisheries, opened the meeting, saying he had come to listen rather than lecture. He turned quickly to land: conflicts between peasants and pastoralists, he said, had killed at least fifteen people across five regions in September alone. He asked MVIWATA to help the government end the land conflicts. Guests included the ambassadors of Cuba and Palestine, the Eastern and Southern Africa Small-Scale Farmers’ Forum, the Tanzanian Socialist Forum, and Pan Africanism Today, which delivered a message of solidarity on behalf of more than seventy movements and organizations in Africa. MVIWATA also read its statement of solidarity with Palestine and Cuba. MVIWATA delegates attending the National Smallholder Farmers’ Conference and the 31st Annual General Meeting of MVIWATA. Photo: MVIWATA Land discussions dominated the first day. Delegates said the courts were out of reach for most peasant farmers. MVIWATA’s chairperson, Apollo Chamwela, told those attending the AGM that in Magungu village in Kiteto, more than sixty farmers had lost their land when it was allocated for grazing. Subira from Msomero and Salum from Rudewa, both in Kilosa district, described village land taken by outsiders with the collusion of the local officials who should have prevented it. “How can the government take the side of the minority against the majority?” Subira asked. “Where should we run to cry?” The second day of the AGM focused on markets: not markets in the abstract, but the system through which smallholders are made to sell their crops. Under Tanzania’s warehouse receipt system, farmers deliver produce to licensed warehouses, usually through cooperative unions, and it is sold by digital auction on a government-controlled exchange rather than at the farm gate. Delegates described a system in which farmers have little say over the floor price, and in which middlemen registered as farmers, “ghost farmers” in the words of MVIWATA Executive Director Stephen Ruvuga, sit where prices are set and gain at the real farmers’ expense. Officials on the platform conceded that small producers outside the cooperative unions are “falling between the cracks.” The session on seeds addressed the regional seed law before the East African Legislative Assembly. The carbon session, the most heated of the three days, heard delegates from Dodoma, Katavi and Kagera describe companies counting trees and signing open-ended contracts with individual farmers who were given no opportunity to understand or scrutinize what they were signing. On the final day, the conference resolutions were adopted by acclamation. MVIWATA will compile its members’ land grievances and submit them to the government through Dr Bashiru Ally, as he had offered. It will expand its legal aid and follow up on cases stalled with officials. It will document flaws in the crop-marketing system, present them to the authorities, build a seedbank dedicated to indigenous seeds, convene an inclusive forum on carbon trade, and track, analyze and critically engage carbon projects and their effects on farmers. Dr Bashiru Ally, Tanzania’s Minister of Livestock and Fisheries, opens the MVIWATA meeting. Photo: MVIWATA The AGM then turned to the organization’s future. Its strategic plan for 2027–2031 will put agroecology first, keep land access as a priority and make a farmers’ bank the next major task, starting with TZS 20 million raised from members themselves. Self-reliance ran through the proceedings: members debated doubling their own annual fee, and left energized to prioritize instruments through which farmers can continue to defend themselves. The meeting closed with the election of the board that will lead MVIWATA for the next three years. In its 33rd year, MVIWATA left Morogoro with a sharper agenda: a dossier of land grievances to present to the government, a seed bank and a farmers’ bank to build with members’ own resources, and a public position on carbon trade. The new leadership’s first test will be whether the government acts on the dossier, and whether members fund what they voted for. Delegates who spoke from the floor are identified by first name and village; office-holders are named in full.’ Jonis Ghedi-Alasow is the Coordinator of the Pan Africanism Today Secretariat.

articles.title: Netanyahu declares full lockdown of West Bank after two Israeli soldiers killed in Hebron
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: Two Palestinian men carried out a shooting attack , targeting a group of Israeli soldiers near the Farsh al-Hawa military checkpoint in the southern West Bank governorate of Hebron on Friday, October 23. According to media reports, the attackers were assassinated by the Israeli forces after engaging in an exchange of fire for about 20 minutes. They were later identified as Firas al-Ju’ba and Hamoudah al-Ju’ba. The attack also resulted in the killing of two Israeli soldiers and the injury of three others. Netanyahu announces refugee-camp model campaign in Hebron and broader West Bank operation In response to the attack, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared a full lockdown in the West Bank and a large-scale operation that will start from the city of Hebron and the neighboring city of Halhul, and further expand to the entire occupied territory. Wearing a bulletproof vest, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threatened from Hebron that the Israeli military will apply the “successful and aggressive model” that the Israeli forces used in the Palestinian refugee camps in the north. The operations in those refugee camps already resulted in the displacement of tens of the thousands of Palestinians, the killing of hundreds, the arrest of over 1,000 , and severe damage and destruction of residential buildings, infrastructure, and properties. “We will evacuate the residents, we will go house to house, remove the weapons there, and all terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed,” Netanyahu threatened. The Israeli military already began to demolish buildings and homes in Hebron shortly after the attack was carried out. Referring to the West Bank as Judea and Samaria, Netanyahu continued: “The defense minister and I have seen plans for a very extensive IDF operation in Judea and Samaria, the likes of which have not been carried out since the Six-Day War.” The Six-Day War was a brief, intense conflict fought between Israel and a coalition of Arab states, primarily Egypt, Syria, and Jordan in 1967. As a result of the war, Israel occupied Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula, Syria’s Golan Heights, the West Bank, and the Gaza Strip. It also forced 300,000 Palestinians and 100,000 Syrians to flee into neighboring countries. It is worth noting that Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz have already threatened a possible war in the West Bank in the last couple of weeks. These threats came hand in hand with an unprecedented escalation of settler violence under the protection of Israeli forces across the occupied territory, alongside intensified military raids. Over 79 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank in 2026, and more than 1,870 others have been injured since the beginning of 2026. Analysts suggest that the escalation in the West Bank aims to push Palestinians towards a confrontation with the Israeli military, a few days before Israel’s legislative elections, scheduled for October 27.

articles.title: Justice for Oscar Belgal
articles.author: Compas de la Diáspora
articles.content: W e join the voices in New York City and the nation in denouncing the most recent ICE shooting and subsequent kidnapping of 28 year old Dominican immigrant and father Oscar Belgal. On October 8, Oscar was surrounded by ICE agents and shot at seven times while in his vehicle during a busy afternoon when many children and parents were around. One of the shots hit his neck. Eyewitnesses describe how he was held by ICE agents and NYPD officers as 20 minutes passed before any ambulance arrived at the crime scene. Oscar was taken to nearby Allen Pavilion hospital and then later kidnapped by ICE agents to an unknown location. We demand his immediate freedom. The shooter has been identified as Kevin Brodowsky. Also on the scene was notorious ICE goon Brenden Cuni who was wearing a construction vest, and was brandishing a AR-15-style rifle, putting the lives of children and passerby at risk. Cuni has terrorized people in NYC (Chinatown, Bushwick, Queens), in Columbus, Ohio, and in Minneapolis, where he participated in the brutal assault and dragging of a pregnant woman across the snowy pavement. Brenden is of Dominican & Puerto Rican descent, which shows that people of any ethnicity can be class traitors and oppressors. We join the mass clamor demanding that Kevin be tried for attempted murder. This reckless act is a continuation of Trump’s murderous and racist anti-immigration policies currently affecting our communities. We condemn the attempts by NYPD commissioner Jessica Tisch and DHS to justify this brutal act by citing Oscar’s previous interactions with the police and his affiliations. This is a blatant act of racism. No criminal record and interaction with the repressive state justifies being shot by ICE in front of your kid. We demand DHS retract that statement and stop criminalizing Dominican and Haitian immigrants as well as Black people and all oppressed immigrant communities. Furthermore, we also condemn Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s inaction for not firing Jessica Tisch and for not having taken steps to disband the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group (SRG) as he promised during his campaign. Instead, Mamdani has allowed the NYPD to continue colluding with ICE, brutalizing protestors who demand the release of our neighbors and demand ICE out of our streets. Mayor Mamdani claims to be on the side of immigrants but actions speak louder than words: we are fed up with promises from “progressive” politicians who are afraid to break their ties with the two-party system and the status quo. As Dominicans in the diaspora, we stand in solidarity with Haitian immigrants and Dominicans of Haitian descent in Dominican Republic, who are also victims of government profiling and repression in the island. What happened to Oscar on October 8, has been happening to Haitian and Black Dominicans for decades in DR. The Dirección General de Migración (DGM) operates as ICE does, raiding public and private spaces and terrorizing neighbors to disappear them into the immigration enforcement system. We stand against ICE the same way we stand against DGM, and all repressive forces. Finally, we call on all workers, parents, high school, and college students in NYC to unite, organize and mobilize, and take part in school walkouts, teach-ins, boycotts, ICE watch in their communities, occupations, strikes, and all actions necessary until NYC is free of ICE terror. We demand: The immediate release of Oscar Belgal to his family Fire Jessica Tisch The end of NYPD collaboration with ICE Mamdani to fulfill his promise to disband the SRG Abolish ICE once and for all Compas de la Diáspora, October 10, 2026 Opinions expressed in signed articles do not necessarily represent the views of the editors or the Tempest Collective. articles.title: Albania’s protests show no signs of backing down
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: The months-long protests in Albania have reached a new escalation, with university students strengthening their mobilization since mid-October. Concerns about study expenses, poor employment prospects, and low wages have added impetus to a movement that has demanded the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama and urgent action on the widespread corruption weighing on the country. “Students have brought the Flamingo Revolution into a new phase,” wrote the Solidarity Albania platform. “In a capital where living costs devour 170% of the median net wage, public universities are starved to force youth into economic exile.” “When a generation rises for its basic rights, the only legitimate response is total solidarity,” they added. “Tirana’s struggle stands shoulder-to-shoulder with student strikes in France and India, and with liberation struggles in Palestine, Sudan, and the Congo, and elsewhere.” Police violence brings comparisons to protests in France Mass mobilizations against elite tourism projects, the devastation of Albania’s natural resources, and corruption have been ongoing since May this year – evolving in what was dubbed the Flamingo Revolution. For the past months, demonstrations have continued on a daily basis, Enriko Peçuli from the progressive party Lëvizja Bashkë told BreakThrough News . “Some days you saw more people on the streets, sometimes a bit less, but gatherings continued basically every night: the energy was there.” On October 13, when the latest upsurge began, “you could sense in the city that something was going to happen,” Peçuli adds. When students assembled in large numbers near the Ministry of Education and part of the building caught fire, police violence erupted, Peçuli says – and has continued for ten days in a row. Read more: Protests banned and curfews declared ahead of next major mobilization in France The authorities’ violent response has drawn comparisons to the institutional response to youth mobilizations in France, yet it represents a new element in local mobilizations. During other significant demonstrations, including the student protests in 2018, it was not as pronounced, Peçuli says – possibly indicating Rama’s worsening position. Ever since the beginning of the protests, the prime minister has tried to deflect responsibility and avoided the protesters’ core demand: his resignation. When the Flamingo Revolution started, Peçuli describes, Rama tried to blame it on foreign powers. He has named the governments of Greece, Iran, and Russia as culprits for the mobilizations. “It’s only gotten worse with time,” the activist points out. “He’s becoming more and more arrogant, he uses a language of violence.” “Rage is pushing people into the streets” After the escalation of the past days, Rama attempted – in a way – to establish dialogue with the students. This was resolutely rejected, as Peçuli notes that protesters will not agree to anything less than the government’s resignation. “It’s spontaneous rage pushing people into the streets,” he said, nodding to the events’ decentralized character that some have credited for at least part of the demonstrations’ longevity. “We don’t have trade unions or big student movements [like the ones in France], society is generally not organized in the same way,” Peçuli points out – but there’s no sign of backing down. “Rama might have offered dialogue, but it’s difficult to take that seriously after the past 10 days. After you’ve sanctioned breaking people’s heads, your right to call for dialogue is a bit limited.”

articles.title: Protests against electoral fraud continue in India
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Thousands of protesters marched to the headquarters of the Election Commission of India (ECI) in Delhi and to other government offices in several cities across India on Friday, October 23, as part of the ongoing nationwide demonstrations against alleged electoral fraud and manipulations. Protesters in Delhi carrying the national flag shouted slogans against the election fraud and the attacks on people’s right to vote, right to protest, and basic democracy in the country. They were stopped by the security forces deployed in large numbers who had barricaded all the routes leading to the ECI office hours before the protests began. Some of the protesters were also detained. Similar protests were held across different parts of the country on Friday and earlier this week . The protests in Delhi were called by People Against SIR, a group of over 300 organizations formed recently to coordinate ongoing protests. The group includes major trade and farmers unions, student and youth movements, and other sections of civil society. A large number of farmers also participated in the protests which have been ongoing since the beginning of the month and are expected to intensify in the coming days as all opposition parties and civil society groups have already called for a large demonstration in Delhi on November 1 over the failure of the government to respond to their demands so far. The march on Friday was converted to a public meeting after it was stopped by the security forces. Several people addressed the protesters, pointing out the complete disregard to the basic rights of citizens by the Narendra Modi-led government. Some of them also questioned the legitimacy of the ultra-right-wing government, claiming it was a result of a stolen mandate. Undeclared emergency The Narendra Modi government has imposed an undeclared emergency in the country by making it an offense to wave the national flag, arresting activists, and letting the police and pro-regime thugs repeatedly attack protesters, women and journalists, People Against SIR said in a press release on Thursday. The failure of the constitutional institutions, including the Supreme Court of India to intervene against the blatant misuse of state power and their failure to protect the basic rights of the people confirms the state of democracy in the country, it underlined. Two leaders of the CJP were sent to seven days of judicial custody after they tried to unfurl the national flag in central Delhi last week in an attempt to resist the government’s clampdown on the protesters. Hundreds of people, mostly young activists, have been detained, and beaten by the security forces since the beginning of the protests. Several of the women protesters and journalists have complained about police and pro-government thugs molesting and beating them during the protests. The government has repeatedly used sections of the law to restrict movement and barricaded the central parts of the capital city for weeks now. India cannot be allowed to become a police state The protesters decried the restrictions imposed by the government against protests in the capital and other places, calling it a violation of the right to peaceful protest. They announced that they will not let India become a “police state.” The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) is an ongoing process initiated by the ECI to revise the electoral rolls in the country. The opposition has alleged that the process was illegal and was initiated with the intention to manipulate elections to benefit the ruling ultra-right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has been in power since 2014. Several reports in the local newspapers have also claimed the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar violated established legal procedures and made changes in the SIR process arbitrarily on several occasions to benefit the ruling party. Over 130 million voters, around 14% of all registered electorates in the country as per the 2024 data, have been removed from India’s decentralized electoral rolls since the process began last year. In some states a quarter to half of all electorates were removed. The number is significant especially given the fact that in India’s First Past the Post system, the victory margins in elections are often very small. Some have claimed that many of the voters removed from the roll were from religious minority communities or sections of the working class which have generally voted against the BJP. One of the major demands of the ongoing protests is the removal of the SIR process altogether. Protesters have also demanded the removal of the sitting CEC and for legal action to be taken against him, as well as the re-inclusion of all the people whose names have been removed from the electoral rolls.

articles.title: Protests banned and curfews declared ahead of next major mobilization in France
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Hundreds of thousands are set to take to the streets in cities across France on Saturday, October 24, once again protesting austerity and the cost of living crisis. Demonstrations are set to go ahead despite an extremely repressive response from the government and local authorities, including curfews and bans . Over the past couple of days, a growing number of cities and regions have announced protest bans, drawing criticism from trade unions and progressive groups. “The government has banned demonstrations on Saturday in Lyon, Marseille, Rouen, Grenoble, Le Havre, Bourg-en-Bresse, Le Mans, Toulon, Chambéry, Perpignan,” wrote Clémence Guetté of La France Insoumise on October 22. “New bans are coming down every hour. Is this what democracy looks like?” Many of the bans are being contested in court, with the final outcome yet to be determined. Read more: Italian government to deploy troops to Milan after anti-austerity protests French President Emmanuel Macron failed to revise his stance on the protests in the same period, announcing that only trade union mobilizations will be allowed on Saturday. “Where they are not organized by trade unions, we will ban them wherever we can,” Macron stated. The government announced the intention of deploying troops to “guard” the demonstrations. The idea was announced after nationwide protests on October 17 – attended by roughly 800,000 people – turned into riots against the erosion of education services and overall living standards . A securitization strategy tested in Kanaky This institutional response has been heavily criticized by progressive forces that joined students on the streets. As Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s administration insisted on framing the mobilization exclusively as a security issue, including in meetings with political parties, left forces denounced the strategy for failing to address concrete issues. Paul Vannier of La France Insoumise said the government was engaging in “a strategy of letting the situation rot,” insisting that it should instead shape a solution to students’ demands. This would include freezing prices, increasing wages, making higher education more accessible, and allocating €10 billion for the education system. Read more: Students in France are fighting for stronger public education The French left has also sounded the alarm about the long-term consequences of the violent repression of the protests: thousands of youth were arrested during the mobilization, and dozens were injured – some of them very seriously. While alarming, this course of events is not surprising, La France Insoumise pointed out. The party compared the repression observed in French cities to the one witnessed during protests in Kanaky in 2024: “a state of emergency, extended curfews, a general ban on demonstrations, the blocking of TikTok, nearly 3,000 security personnel deployed with army support, armored vehicles, and the massive use of LBD launchers and grenades.” “What the state tested in 2024 in Kanaky, it is now applying in 2026 to its own youth, with the same men in charge,” the media outlet L’Insoumission wrote. Trade unions’ support continues It is in this context that progressive forces in France have reiterated calls for the public to respond to the students’ call and protect their right to protest on Saturday. “On October 24, we once again call on all activists to put on their red [trade union] vests so that young people and workers can exercise their right to demonstrate and to make their demands heard,” the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) wrote. Students, trade unions, and progressive groups are mobilizing against austerity, the cost of living crisis, and eroding conditions in education. Source: CGT/Facebook “We are witnessing an authoritarian shift that goes hand in hand with the government’s stubborn refusal to own up to its record and to call into question its unjust policy in favor of the wealthiest,” dozens of trade unionists, advocates, and cultural workers wrote in an appeal , calling for support for the protests. “This choice is irresponsible and dangerous for democracy, and for the physical integrity of those who defend it without the framework of these mobilizations,” they stated. “It paves the way for the far right to come to power.”
